10148-the-merry-adventures-of-robin-hood:
Howard Pyle's Merry Adventures of Robin Hood opens with an address to the reader, warning serious folk who think life has nothing to do with innocent laughter to close the book. Those who go on will meet good, sober folk of real history frisking in gay colors, including a stout, lusty Henry II and a fair, gentle lady.

Set in merry England in the time of old King Henry the Second, the tales follow Robin from the greenwood dawn of Maytime through outlawry, friendship, and archery. Pyle's pictures and prose made this the classic Robin Hood. Readers of all ages get the outlaw at his merriest and most generous.
10321-dragon-s-blood:
Henry Milner Rideout published this romance in 1909, with pictures by Harold M. Brett. Its opening letter nods to Kipling's tale of Kafiristan, then promises a slighter, stranger bag of tricks. The story moves between town life, pagodas, and war boards, with a lady, a griffin, and a pied piper among its early signs.

Sword play, a hot night, a siege, and a figure called Kau Fai carry the plot through peril and intrigue. Love, loyalty, and honor thread the action, in the manner of early twentieth-century adventure fiction. Readers get a colorful, fast-moving romance of the exotic East, told with verve.
10463-the-little-house-in-the-fairy-wood:
Ethel Cook Eliot wrote this children's fantasy for Torka and Northwind, opening on a cold morning when Eric is shaken awake by Mrs. Freg at six o'clock. Eric shares a bed with two other boys, and his day begins like any other, yet it will become the beginning of all things new. The fairy wood waits beyond the house.

Magic in a mist, a bright house, firelight, gossip, world stories, and a witch at the window fill later chapters. Tree mothers, wind hunts, and spring wanderings carry Eric deeper into wonder. Readers get a gentle, lyrical fantasy of childhood, nature, and magic.
10846-seekers-after-god:
F. W. Farrar, canon of Westminster, wrote Seekers After God about pagan thinkers who reached toward truths Christianity would later proclaim. The book opens with Seneca of Cordova, on the Baetis under the Sierra Morena, in a city Augustus honored as the Patrician Colony. Spain gave Rome emperors Trajan, Hadrian, and Theodosius, and writers from Columella to Quintilian.

Farrar sets Seneca among Stoics who sought a higher life through reason, duty, and self-command. His tone is reverent and scholarly, quoting a French critic on Seneca's cloud fringed with rays. Readers get a humane study of philosophy on the edge of faith.
10889-the-life-and-romances-of-mrs-eliza:
George Frisbie Whicher wrote this 1915 study of Eliza Haywood, a prolific London novelist of the early 1700s. Haywood left almost no record of her own life, so Whicher builds her story from scant facts, her books, and contemporary gossip. Chapters trace her from short romances of passion through scandal novels and secret histories to later domestic fiction.

Along the way, Whicher explains her part in the Duncan Campbell pamphlets, her attack by Pope in The Dunciad, and her essays and letters. He also judges which works matter and why her reputation faded. The monograph suits readers of early English fiction, offering both a life pieced together from fragments and a clear guide to a very large body of work.
11044-the-existence-of-god:
Francois de Salignac de la Mothe-Fenelon, Archbishop of Cambrai, argued for God's existence in this classic work, here in an English translation transcribed by David Price. Fenelon admits that metaphysical proofs, tracing things to first principles, suit few minds, since their very simplicity escapes those unused to pure thought. Moral proofs, drawn from nature, suit everyone.

Opening the eyes, Fenelon says, shows art throughout nature, and wisdom stamped on all creatures points to a maker, just as the soul's power over the body points beyond itself. St. Augustine's reflections on the body and soul support the case. The book offers a gentle, popular philosophy of religion, aimed at readers who reason from what they see rather than from abstract ideas.
11097-young-robin-hood:
G. Manville Fenn wrote this boys' adventure about Robin Hood as a boy, with twenty-three illustrations. Young Robin rides behind a sour serving man named David, wriggling on a slippery horse through a dark forest of oak and beech. David warns of robbers, and Robin answers that he would like to meet Robin Hood himself.

Forest pools, golden carp, pike, and dragonflies fill the journey, and Robin's boldness marks him out early. Fenn imagines the outlaw's childhood as a tale of courage, humour, and woodland adventure, suitable for young readers. The book gives the Robin Hood legend a fresh start, with a boy hero learning the forest before he leads its men.
11268-the-flood:
Part of the Old Testament Scenes and Narratives series, a second series of the Good Child's Library, this 1851 Philadelphia children's book retells the Flood in fifteen short chapters. Contents move from the wickedness of man and Noah's command to build the ark. through the opening windows of heaven and the floating ark, to the raven and dove, Noah's sacrifice, and the bow in the clouds. Illustrations in oil colors accompanied the text.

Hogan, Perkins and Company planned the series to match their New Testament volumes, offering children a scriptural library in uniform style. The Flood's language is simple and its episodes brief, suited to reading aloud. For historians of children's publishing, it shows Bible stories packaged as attractive, illustrated gift books.
12038-representative-plays-by-american-d:
Montrose J. Moses's Representative Plays by American Dramatists, 1856 to 1911, edited with an introduction to each play, appeared in 1921 with portraits and original playbills. Moses dedicates the volume to Brander Matthews, friend of the American theatre, to whom all critics of the theatre are beholden.

The table of contents opens with an introduction and bibliographies, then Rip Van Winkle, a legend of the Catskills, in a comparative arrangement with the Kerr version. Moses's anthology argues, by selection, that American drama had a history worth studying, from melodrama and comedy to the more serious plays of the early twentieth century.
12475-fires-of-driftwood:
Isabel Ecclestone MacKay's verse collection, first published in Toronto in 1922, gathers poems that had appeared in magazines from Harper's and Scribner's to Canadian journals. Decorations by J. E. H. MacDonald frame lyrics with titles such as Fires of Driftwood, When as a Lad, A Pilgrim and The Homesteader.

Nature, seasons and travel supply much of the imagery, from spring and autumn gardens to wet weather and a crocus bed. Other poems turn to loss, fear, resurrection and a lost name, keeping a reflective, often Canadian, note. The volume reads as a working poet's harvest, magazine pieces brought together into one book of short, musical lyrics.
13526-in-the-clutch-of-the-war-god:
Milo Hastings imagines a future war in this tale from Physical Culture magazine, July to September 1911, framed as the Humaniculture Society's history of the twentieth century. The Orient invades the Occident, and America, self-satisfied and deaf to lessons of Oriental progress, faces the cost of complacency.

Ethel watches a great squadron move eastward, with men and women trained as aviators and a fan-ventilated gymnasium as the ship's most conspicuous fitting. Cities drop conflagration bombs on shingled roofs and prussic acid into reservoirs, while an American army gathers in a giant semicircle from coast to coast. Hastings writes invasion fiction as warning, not celebration.
13775-every-step-in-canning-the-cold-pac:
Grace Viall Gray, a former home economics teacher at Iowa State College, wrote this 1920 manual on canning. It teaches the cold-pack method step by step, from getting ready to storing finished jars. Chapters cover soft fruits, hard fruits, vegetables, soups, jellies, meat, and fish. Later sections add drying, brining, curing, and home storage.

Gray stresses clean jars, correct heat, and safe seals. She explains why canned goods spoil and how to prevent it. Tips on racks, jar holders, and marketing home-canned food help beginners and sellers alike. The book reflects wartime thrift and the rise of home science teaching. It remains a clear, practical guide to preserving food at home.
13916-marie-bashkirtseff-from-childhood-:
Mary J. Safford translated this selection from Marie Bashkirtseff's journals, covering childhood to girlhood. Bashkirtseff began writing at twelve, ingenuously and sincerely, amusing readers with whims and touching them with sufferings. Notebooks bound in white parchment, slightly discoloured, held her early writing. Editors chose first books for their revelation of a young girl's mind.

Marie prays for blessings and for love, imagining a beloved dead with tears in her eyes. Her enthusiasms, vanities, and sorrows fill the pages. The journal later made her famous as an artist and diarist who died young. This volume suits readers of diaries and women's lives. It shows a gifted girl thinking aloud.
13982-cap-n-abe-storekeeper-a-story-of-c:
James A. Cooper wrote Cap'n Abe, Storekeeper in 1917, a Cape Cod story of shop, sea, and romance. Cap'n Abe runs his store and living room, where neighbours gather. Chapters follow a choice, a shadow of coming events, and what happened in the night. Boarded by pirates, suspicion, and salt water taffy add humour.

Louise Grayling, hobbled by city life for nearly a year, craves new scenes and gives up a furnished apartment. Aunt Euphemia descends, Washy Gallup grows curious, and discoveries follow. Cooper writes Cape Cod speech and custom with affection. The novel suits readers of regional romance. Its storekeeper hero anchors a warm community tale.
14026-spiritual-life-and-the-word-of-god:
Emanuel Swedenborg's Spiritual Life and the Word of God, extracted from Apocalypse Explained, sets out his theology in three parts. Part one treats spiritual life: how it is acquired, goods of charity, shunning evils, and cleansing the inside. Part two expounds the commandments one by one. Part three treats profanations of good and truth.

Swedenborg argues that church building and hospitals count as good only when done without hope of reward. Works done by man alone, or for reward, fail his test. The book presents Swedenborgian doctrine in systematic form. It suits readers of mysticism and Christian thought. The extracts offer a clear entry to a difficult author.
14076-the-elephant-god:
A rogue elephant in the Terai forest sets Gordon Casserly's 1921 adventure in motion, starting from a secret mission. Dedicated to a real killer elephant, the book follows Major Dermot through rajahs' palaces, Bhuttia raids, and the rescue of Noreen. A girl of the Terai, a rajah who covets an Englishwoman, and a feast of the goddess Kali raise the stakes chapter by chapter.

Love tangles with empire politics. The Rajah of Lalpuri, thwarted by his Dewan, demands the girl he saw at a durbar in Jalpaiguri and hires clever men to find a way. Dermot dances, sups, and hides in cardrooms while danger gathers. Casserly knew the frontier world he staged, and the novel moves at adventure pace: elephants, temples, palaces of death, and a tempest. Romance and peril share the work evenly throughout.
14563-sheila-of-big-wreck-cove-a-story-o:
James A. Cooper's 1922 Cape Cod story centers on Sheila of Big Wreck Cove, a girl caught in the life of a fishing village of captains, Portuguese workers, and summer visitors. The book first ran as a serial in 1921.

Cap'n Ira and Prue open the tale, and chapters follow the captain of the Seamew and the Latham house. A harvest home festival brings Tunis, a friendly local who helps a newcomer's niece settle with the Balls. Cooper writes with affection for Cape speech and shore life. The novel is a warm regional romance, salted with wreck lore and village gossip.
14566-elsie-s-motherhood:
Martha Finley's Elsie's Motherhood, the fifth Elsie volume, published in 1876, continues Elsie's life into motherhood in the South of 1867 and 1868. The preface notes that Ku Klux doings were added for a truer picture of those years.

Elsie guides her children Vi and others with prayer, tears, and gentle correction, urging kind thoughts toward cousins and gifts from pocket money. The household scenes are warm and pious, in Finley's familiar manner. The book pleased the series' many admirers, and it shows Reconstruction-era domestic fiction from a conservative Southern viewpoint. Finley's readers followed Elsie from girlhood to motherhood.
14573-the-truce-of-god:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's short 1920 tale is set in a medieval town at Christmas, where the Church's Truce of God forbids fighting from Thursday evening to Monday morning. The town celebrates with a roast steer, fruit, and vegetables.

A young overlord sulks in his cliff-top castle, nursing a grievance, while a bishop seeks to soften him and teach what matters beyond war and pride. Rinehart writes the legend in simple, tender prose, with illustrations by Harold Sichel. The story preaches peace at the year's darkest festival, and it remains a gentle holiday fable.
14874-elsie-s-womanhood:
Martha Finley's Elsie's Womanhood, a sequel to Elsie's Girlhood, was called for so loudly that the author undertook it with pleasure. Dates compelled bringing in the late war, the American Civil War, and Finley strives to wound no feelings, to stay as impartial as if writing history.

Her aim is a true, though faint, picture of great losses and sufferings on both sides. She hopes the thought of renewing the awful strife will become utterly abhorrent to every lover of peace. Elsie, now a woman, faces war, family and faith with the moral steadiness readers knew from her girlhood. The complete authorised edition keeps that earnest, domestic tone intact.
14946-the-blossoming-rod:
Mary Stewart Cutting's short Christmas story follows Mr. Langshaw, who senses unusual preparations for a gift to him this year. Children keep asking him for change to pay for services rendered, and dollars and cents enter the family's Christmas festivities as they enter daily life.

Langshaw stops as usual to look at a sporting goods display on his way home, on the Friday before Christmas Monday. He touches a ten-dollar bill in his pocket and wonders what the gift will be. A rod flapped in circles in the backyard, shown in an illustration, hints at the answer. Cutting writes a gentle tale of family calculation, affection and a present that blossoms beyond its price.
14961-sentimental-tommy-the-story-of-his:
J. M. Barrie's 1896 story of Tommy's boyhood opens with Tommy contriving to keep one out, first seen on a dirty London stair at five, in sexless garments that were all he had. He must be looked at sideways, lest he sit down hurriedly to hide them.

That inscrutable face, which later made clubmen uneasy and puzzled ladies while he made love to them, is already his, except when he smiles at a pretty face. Barrie, author of The Little Minister and A Window in Thrums, follows Tommy from London to Thrums and through a boyhood of sentiment, mischief and imagination. The novel is a portrait of a future writer in the making.
15583-adventures-of-buffalo-bill-from-bo:
Colonel Prentiss Ingraham wrote this dime novel of Buffalo Bill. Beadle and Adams of New York published it weekly in 1881. It was number one of Beadle's Boy's Library of Sport, Story and Adventure. It cost five cents, at two dollars fifty a year, and promised truth stranger than fiction. The subtitle calls Cody the monarch of bordermen.

Deeds of daring, scenes of thrilling peril, and romantic incidents trace Cody's early life from boyhood to manhood. An illustration shows a maddened bull bounding into the air, goring those in advance, and leading the herd. The prologue opens by insisting truth beats fiction. The book is classic dime-novel biography: a frontier hero built for boys, in fast, breathless episodes of danger and pluck.
15622-handbook-on-japanning-2nd-edition-:
William N. Brown wrote this handbook on japanning for ironware, tinware, wood, and more, with sections on tin-plating and galvanizing. Scott, Greenwood and Son of London published the second edition, revised and enlarged with thirteen illustrations, in January 1913, with D. Van Nostrand in New York. The first edition, under the title A Handbook on Japanning and Enamelling, appeared in 1901.

Four sections cover the craft in order. The introduction teaches priming and preparing surfaces, and a first stage for wood or leather without priming. Japan grounds follow in white, blue, scarlet, red, yellow, green, orange, purple, and black, with tortoise-shell ground, painting, and varnishing. Japanning metals, enamelling bedstead frames, and japanning tin trays close the early sections. The book is a practical trade manual for a decorative craft now largely lost.
1564-boswell-s-life-of-johnson-abridged-:
James Boswell's Life of Johnson, here abridged and edited by Charles Grosvenor Osgood of Princeton, follows Samuel Johnson through London coffee houses, Grub Street hack work. The making of his great Dictionary. Boswell, Johnson's young Scottish friend, records his talk, his quarrels, and his kindnesses with unmatched fidelity.

Osgood's abridgement cuts most legal opinions, many letters, and Boswell's own notes, keeping the conversations and scenes that show Johnson alive. The result is a shorter road into a very long classic. It remains the best first version of the most famous biography in English.
15652-the-poetical-works-of-thomas-hood:
William Michael Rossetti edited this enlarged and revised edition of the poetical works of Thomas Hood, published in New York by A. L. Burt Company. Rossetti's biographical introduction opens by noting how few outward events marked Hood's life: life-long ill health, and one commercial failure with consequent expatriation. Beyond that, little presents itself for record in an upright, beneficial career, bright with genius and wit, dark with death's lengthening shadow.

Contents run from To Hope, The Departure of Summer, and The Sea of Death through Lycus the Centaur, Fair Ines, and sonnets on silence and death. I Remember, I Remember, The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies, and Hero and Leander follow. Hood's father, a London publisher and bookseller, reprinted old works and published Bloomfield. The volume gathers a beloved Victorian poet's lyrics, ballads, and comic verse in one place.
15933-stories-of-childhood:
A children's anthology in the Little Classics series, edited by Rossiter Johnson, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1914. Copyright dates to 1875, with James R. Osgood and Company. Johnson gathers tales of childhood by famous hands, each short enough for reading aloud. The Riverside Press printed the volume.

A Dog of Flanders by Ouida leads, with Ruskin's King of the Golden River and Elizabeth Stuart Phelps's Lady of Shalott. Marjorie Fleming by John Brown, Little Jakey, and Henry Kingsley's Lost Child follow, with John Neal, Rebecca Harding Davis, and Dickens's Child's Dream of a Star. The book gives a Victorian shelf of childhood: tender, moral, and made to be remembered.
16180-roman-mosaics-or-studies-in-rome-a:
Hugh Macmillan's Roman Mosaics, published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1888, studies Rome and its neighborhood in linked essays. Chapter one walks to church in Rome. It passes a country walk and a town residence, the Piazza di Spagna, the staircase, and beggars. Flowers, the Via Babuino, and the Pincian Hill lead on to the Villa Borghese and Ponte Molle. Chapter two takes the Appian Way, its tombs, its lonely country, and its gates.

Macmillan, author of Bible Teachings in Nature, joins travel, history, and devotion in a minister's observant voice. Each mosaic piece sets a Roman scene beside a reflection. Readers planning an armchair visit to Rome will find a warm, learned companion.
16478-records-of-a-girlhood:
Frances Ann Kemble, the famed actress, draws on thousands of her own letters, written over forty years, for this 1880 memoir. Portions first ran in the Atlantic Monthly, with much new matter added and the whole revised. The girlhood chapters recall her youth, her stage life, and the people who shaped her.

Kemble writes with frankness and wit, and the letters give the book a direct, personal voice. Theater history, family life, and social scenes of the early nineteenth century all pass through her pages. Readers who like memoirs built from real letters will find this one vivid and unguarded.
16585-charred-wood:
Myles Muredach's 1917 novel opens with the Lady of the Tree and a monsignore, then winds through suspicion, Killimaga, bitter bread, and a bishop's confession. Who is Ruth, and why does a duchess abdicate, are the puzzles at the center, with an abduction, thin ice, and a beckoning hand along the way. The title asks whether God must char wood before He can draw with it.

The tale mixes Catholic atmosphere with mystery and romance, in the popular style of its day. The pace is brisk, the scenes shift from cliffs to confessionals, and the close ties the threads. Readers of old-fashioned mystery romance will find it colorful and absorbing.
16591-unity-of-good:
Mary Baker Eddy, author of Science and Health, sets out Christian Science teaching in this volume, copyrighted 1887, 1891, and 1908. Contents ask whether God knows sin, sickness, and death, whether anything real meets the physical senses, and whether there is death. A credo closes the questions: belief in God, man, matter, woman, and evil, with a summary of unity of good.

Eddy writes as a religious founder stating doctrine plainly for followers. The book is short and systematic, meant for study rather than casual reading. Readers of American religion will find a core text of Christian Science in its author's own words.
17434-the-thin-red-line-and-blue-blood:
Arthur Griffiths, author of chronicles of Newgate prison, issued this two-volume novel in London in 1886. The first volume opens in Paris, where a commissary is called, an arrest follows, and talk of war grows until soldiers head off to fight. Battles, a costly victory, a November gale, and the Golden Horn carry the action through courts, camps, and high society.

The second volume turns to secret service work, Cossacks, a fortress, Paris, Lincoln's Inn, and married life, closing with a short piece called Blue Blood. Readers get a broad Victorian war and intrigue novel, mixing battle scenes with spying, family ties, and social rank. Its sweep across two volumes gives the period a full stage.
18896-faith-gartney-s-girlhood:
Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney wrote this novel of a girl's growing up, issued in New York in 1913 by the New York Book Company. Whitney was known for The Gayworthys and A Summer in Leslie Goldthwaite's Life. The chapters trace Faith Gartney from money worries and sortes through aunts, neighbors, and new duties, toward a niche in life and a woman to fill it.

Along the way come a drive with the doctor, frost wonders, snow, a game at chess, and questions answered in conflict. Whitney's heroine learns through work, care for others, and patient endurance. Readers get a wholesome, old-fashioned novel of girlhood, written for young women, with a warm view of family, friendship, and moral growth.
19418-confessions-of-boyhood:
John Albee wrote this memoir of a New England boyhood, published in the early nineteen hundreds. Short chapters recall a small house, school days, church funerals, woods and pastures, and the long shadow of the Dorr War and the Millerite stir. His mother, his uncle, and the working men around him all stand out in clear portraits.

Later chapters follow the boy into trades: the sawmill, bootmaking, shop work, teaching, and farm labor. The book is less a life story in full than a set of scenes from youth, kept for what they show of work, faith, and home in rural America.
1965-captain-blood:
Rafael Sabatini's Captain Blood follows Peter Blood, an Irish doctor sold into slavery in Barbados after the Monmouth Rebellion. He escapes with fellow slaves to become the most feared pirate of the Caribbean. Blood's honor, his surgery, and his sword carry him through battles, betrayals, and a love affair with the governor's niece.

Sabatini writes the pirate romance with dash and with care for ships, law, and medicine. Blood himself — a gentleman forced into piracy — gives the book its moral center. The novel made Sabatini famous, and it remains the model for every pirate hero who is really a gentleman in disguise.
19805-the-tale-of-mr-tod:
Beatrix Potter published The Tale of Mr. Tod in 1912. Mr. Tod is a fox, and Tommy Brock is a badger. Brock only occasionally eats rabbit pie, the tale confides. He takes very little young ones when other food is really scarce. Brock and old Mr. Bouncer share a dislike of the wicked otters and Mr. Tod. They often talk over that painful subject together.

Mr. Tod is among Potter's darkest tales. Benjamin Bunny's children are stolen for a fox's supper. Tommy Brock, no hero himself, becomes the rescue. Potter wrote it for older children and kept the danger real. Her watercolors and prose stay exact and unsentimental. It is a summit of her art.
20157-the-call-of-the-blood:
Robert Hichens published The Call of the Blood in 1905, a novel of love and fate. A woman takes letters from her writing-table drawer with care. She awaits a visit from their writer, Emile Artois, that day. He has wired that he comes from Paris by night train and boat.

Hichens sets much of the tale in Sicily, under a hot southern sun. The call of the blood means deep pulls of race, place, and passion. His characters feel forces they can barely name or resist. Readers get lush, tense romance in the style that made Hichens famous.
20219-the-lion-s-brood:
Duffield Osborne published The Lion's Brood in 1901, a novel of ancient Rome. A man wakes to find a coin turned in his hand as he dozed. Its reverse shows a horseman in full armor at the gallop. The rider brandishes a naked sword and grips a severed head by its hair.

That grim coin sets the tone for a tale of Rome's hard men. Osborne wrote of eagles, legions, and the brood that Rome bred for war. Battles and honor codes drive his Romans far more than ease. Readers get a vivid, blood-stained romance of the ancient world.
20846-handwork-in-wood:
Thanks to tool firms in New Haven, Chicago, and Beloit open William Noyes's Handwork in Wood. Their loan of electrotypes helped the book's many plates take shape. Stanley Rule and Level of New Britain stands among those thanked by name.

Noyes, a teacher at Teachers College, wrote a full guide to wood craft. Timber, tools, joints, and design unfold in set order with clear plates. The book served school shops that taught hand skill as mind training. Its mix of craft lore and teaching method still speaks to woodworkers who learn best by doing, step by careful step.
21074-afloat-on-the-flood:
Lawrence J. Leslie set this boys' novel in the town of Carson, where spring rain has sent the Evergreen River on the rampage. Published in Chicago in 1915, it follows young Max and his friends as floodwater rises around their homes. Chapters move from weather reports at the post office to rescues on a shaking bridge.

The boys lend a helping hand, shelter in a half-drowned farmhouse, and take refuge on a roof. Later they defend their camp against a wild dog pack and face unwelcome guests. The flood itself is the main villain, and the story ends as the waters fall.
2142-childhood:
Leo Tolstoy begins his semi-autobiographical trilogy with Childhood, translated by C. J. Hogarth, opening on a boy's tenth birthday in August. His tutor Karl Ivanitch wakes him by slapping the wall with a fly-flap, knocking a dead fly onto his curls. Tolstoy wrote Childhood in the 1850s, drawing on his own boyhood at Yasnaya Polyana.

From that small scene Tolstoy builds a whole world of family, servants, lessons, and first feelings, told with exact memory. The book charms by its honesty about a child's mind, and it points toward the great novels that followed. The tutor Karl Ivanitch, kind and foolish by turns, stands for the child's first view of adults.
21697-the-red-man-s-revenge-a-tale-of-th:
R. M. Ballantyne sets The Red Man's Revenge on the Red River, in a tale tied to a great flood. Ballantyne served as a clerk of the Hudson's Bay Company at the Red River Settlement from 1841. He worked there until 1847 and came home to Edinburgh in 1848.

His letters home, full of backwoods life, pushed his family to urge a book. The Young Fur Traders, Ungava, and The Coral Island grew from that start. In his last years his pen slowed, though his quality never failed. This tale returns to the ground he knew best, the northern Canadian settlement of his youth.
22012-the-rover-boys-on-a-hunt-or-the-my:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, wrote The Rover Boys on a Hunt for the long Rover Boys series. It appeared in 1920. Jack Rover and his cousins are finishing the term at Putnam Hall when the story opens with a bobsled race. Christmas at home and a railroad rescue follow before the boys head north to Cedar Lodge.

Winter camp gives them hunting, ice fishing, and unwelcome visitors. Wolves prowl the woods, and a strange house deep in the trees raises questions no one can answer at first. The boys meet each scrape with jokes and teamwork. It is a brisk sample of the series fiction American boys devoured a century ago.
23223-good-blood: Ernst von Wildenbruch's Good Blood opens in a pleasant town known for its retired gentlemen. One of them, an old retired colonel, is known to everyone in town. He belongs to a colony of the superannuated, men who have settled down in this agreeable place to drag out the end of their days, wearily, in retirement.
23545-songs-of-childhood:
Walter Ramal, better known as Walter de la Mare, wrote these songs of childhood. They were first printed in nineteen hundred two by Longmans, Green, and here in a Garland facsimile from a Yale copy. Forty seven poems on subjects and experiences familiar to children fill the book, with a preface by Anthony Hecht.

De la Mare follows the Romantic dream that a child is both the most innocent and the wisest of us all, a theme Wordsworth hailed in his mighty prophet lines. The poems speak of play, fear, wonder, and small daily sights in a voice both simple and strange. Young readers and grown lovers of verse alike will enjoy the songs, which treat childhood not as a lesser age but as a clear, bright way of seeing.
23564-rookwood:
William Harrison Ainsworth wrote this novel of Rookwood, praised by Thackeray as immortal and by the New York Herald for vivid pictures of times and places. A memoir to his mother opens the book, followed by the wedding ring, a vault, a skeleton hand, the park, the hall, and Sir Reginald and Sir Piers Rookwood.

Ranulph Rookwood, Lady Rookwood, a chamber of death, and feuding brothers drive the plot, with Dick Turpin clearing Hornsey toll gate in a famed plate. Ainsworth mixes gothic horror, highwayman dash, and family curse in a tale that made his name. Readers who love old melodrama will enjoy Rookwood's vaults, secrets, and gallops, told with a gusto that still carries a reader along.
2450-boyhood:
Leo Tolstoy's Boyhood, the second part of his autobiographical trilogy, follows the young narrator from childhood into adolescence, with its confusions, friendships, and moral awakenings. The book traces school, family, and first love with the psychological honesty that would fill Tolstoy's great novels. Its episodes are small, but their feeling is large.

The trilogy's middle volume shows Tolstoy learning his art: memory rendered as moral inquiry. Readers approaching his work will find a short, accessible start. It pairs with Childhood and Youth. Tolstoy wrote the trilogy between his army service and his great novels.
25118-when-grandmamma-was-new-the-story-:
Marion Harland's When Grandmamma Was New, published in Boston in 1899, gathers childhood memories of Virginia. Harland told them to her grandsons over library fires on autumn and winter evenings. The title comes from a small boy, Fritz, who said he liked best to hear about what happened when Grandmamma was new.

Stories recall a girlhood of family discipline, first lies and their punishment, and beaux in borrowed clothes. They capture the small dramas of a Southern household before the Civil War. Harland tells them with warmth and humor, and the book reads as both a family keepsake and a gentle record of Virginia domestic life.
25547-the-sundering-flood:
William Morris writes this unfinished romance, printed in volume twenty-one of his Collected Works by Longmans in 1914. A river called the Sundering Flood gives the tale its name and its shape, dividing folk who dwell on its banks.

Chapters follow Wethermel and the child Osberne, wolves harrying the flock, Surly John quarrelling with the goodman, and Osberne slaying the wolves. Later chapters bring a newcomer with a gift, a guest called Waywearer, and Steelhead giving Osberne the sword Boardcleaver. Osberne and Elfhild hold converse across the flood that keeps them apart.
25928-norman-vallery-or-how-to-overcome-:
W. H. G. Kingston tells how a spoiled boy learns goodness, in a tale of Victorian childhood with many pictures. Norman Vallery, about seven or less, has been raised by his soldier father in India to believe he may do exactly as he wishes. The result is a most unpleasant child, unkind to beasts, to his sister, and to all around him, and the pictures drive the point home with skill.

Norman and his parents sail to England, where his sister was sent years before to live with a kind grandmother. At first he behaves intolerably, but steady kindness from others starts to change him. Hurt by his own fault in a grave mishap, he is saved by a child he wronged, and at a proper boarding school he earns top marks for conduct. Kindness, the book says, pays better than willfulness.
26145-the-tell-el-amarna-period:
Carl Niebuhr's short study, translated by J. Hutchinson and issued in London in 1903, explains Egypt's ties with western Asia in the 1400s BC through the Tell el Amarna tablets. It opens with the ruined city on the Nile's east bank, between Minieh and Siut. Local finders came on chests of clay tablets, broke the largest for sale, and drew the government in.

Chapters cover the tablets and their finding, the Egyptian court, letters from Asiatic kings, and letters from vassals. Later pages show how scribes worked in Babylonian, the shared tongue of diplomacy. Some wrote with skill, some barely at all, and their letters reveal the politics of the age.
26560-jim-spurling-fisherman-or-making-g:
Albert W. Tolman published this boys' book in 1918, following Graffam Academy seniors Jim Spurling, Roger Lane, and Winthrop Stevens into a summer of fishing work. A smashed start gives way to a fresh start at Tarpaulin Island and a camp at Sprowl's Cove, where the boys learn the trade from the water up. Twenty-four chapters carry them through the season.

They trawl for hake, go swordfishing with lance in hand, and face fog, midnight marauders, and a rebellion in camp. Fists, fireworks, and a lost alumnus test their grit, while pulling together turns the tide. The frontispiece shows Jim dragging himself toward the rock where his father is fastened. It is a working summer story about earning the title of fisherman.
26598-seasoning-of-wood:
Joseph B. Wagner, author of Cooperage, published this treatise with D. Van Nostrand at New York in 1917. It covers the natural and artificial processes used to prepare lumber for manufacture, with detailed notes on uses, characteristics, and properties. Wagner writes for millmen, woodworkers, and builders who need dry, stable wood rather than green stock that warps and splits.

Sections move from timber and tree kinds, coniferous and broad-leaved, through grain, color, odor, weight, and figure, to the enemies of wood such as beetles and borers. Water in wood, the fibre-saturation point, and the advantages of seasoning lead to kiln-drying theory and types of dry kilns. It is a thorough workshop manual from the age of steam kilns and air yards.
2670-love-songs-of-childhood:
Eugene Field wrote these love songs of childhood for his aunt, Mrs. Belle Angler, recalling how she rocked him to sleep singing petty songs. Field tells her she was beautiful then, and more beautiful now, after years of maternity's joys and sorrows.

The poems that follow sing of babies, play, bedtime, and small wonders, in Field's tender, musical voice. They made him a favorite of American nurseries, and many were set to memory by generations of children. The book endures as a gentle classic of verse for the very young.
27067-the-fixed-period:
Anthony Trollope's The Fixed Period, first published anonymously in Blackwood's Magazine in 1882, imagines Britannula, a bright and orderly British colony. It has set up for itself like New Zealand and the Australias. Its people live alone for thirty years, repudiating no debt and trying no communism.

Britannula's great doctrine gives the book its name: citizens, at a fixed age, must give up life in the college, a law first met with ridicule in Britain and then dismay. Through Gabriel Crasweller, Jack Neverbend, and a cricket match, Trollope turns a strange law into a study of duty, family, and freedom.
27978-commentary-on-genesis-vol-2-luther:
John Nicholas Lenker translated this second volume of Luther's commentary on Genesis, Luther on Sin and the Flood, published in Minneapolis by the Luther Press in 1910. The volume covers chapters four to nine of Genesis and appears in English for the first time.

Subjects include Cain's murder and punishment, the wickedness of the old world, the ark, Noah's obedience, the universal destruction, the rainbow covenant, and Ham cursed with Shem and Japheth blessed. Lenker presents Luther as the Gospel Luther, proving evangelical faith as old as Genesis itself. Lenker dedicates the volume to all interested in studying Christian missionary problems of the last times.
28345-somehow-good:
William de Morgan's 1908 novel Somehow Good opens with a penniless traveller who is struck down in London and wakes with his memory gone. Taken in at Krakatoa Villa, he stays on as a stranger nobody can name, finding work and friends while his past remains blank.

Around him move Sally Nightingale, her mother Rosalind, and their neighbours, whose talk, music, and family secrets slowly pull the stranger's history back into view. De Morgan mixes comedy, mystery, and domestic life, letting small clues, old gardens, and half-remembered songs carry the plot toward a wedding and a reckoning with the past.
28700-robin-hood:
Robin Hood, illustrated by N. C. Wyeth and published by David McKay of Philadelphia in 1917, retells the outlaw's adventures. Wyeth's plates show Robin and his mother going to Nottingham Fair, Robin wrestling Will Stuteley at Gamewell, and Robin meeting Maid Marian. Little John fights the sheriff's cook, Robin defeats Nat of Nottingham at quarter-staff, and a last arrow flies from a window.

The tale opens with Master Hugh Fitzooth, King's Ranger at Locksley, finding his boy cutting arrows. Dame Fitzooth brings news: George of Gamewell invites Robin to the fair, and Norman blood against Saxon pride sharpens the talk. Readers get the greenwood legend, told for young readers and richly pictured.
28994-latin-pronunciation-a-short-exposi:
Harry Thurston Peck, professor at Columbia College, wrote this short manual, Latin Pronunciation: A Short Exposition of the Roman Method, in a second, augmented edition from Henry Holt in 1894. Peck wrote for students who had accepted the Roman method on the grammars' authority, but lacked time to learn its arguments or were put off by specialist technicalities.

The manual gives the main facts in simple form: sources of information, the Latin alphabet, sounds of letters and diphthongs, and a short bibliography. Peck notes that every Latinist of standing in Europe and America now approves the Roman method, as giving the speech of educated Romans of the Augustan age. Students get a clear, brief guide to sounding Latin as Romans did.
29152-fifty-glimpses-of-washington-and-i:
Rand, McNally and Company published this picture book of Washington in 1896, copyrighted in 1895. Fifty views, reproduced from recent photographs, show the capital as visitors saw it at the end of the nineteenth century. The Capitol appears from east and west, along with the Mall, the Botanical Garden, and Pennsylvania Avenue.

Other views cover the Senate chamber, the House hall, the Treasury Department, the White House, the Washington Monument, the Potomac River, and statues such as the bronze Garfield at the Capitol grounds. With brief captions rather than long text, the book works as a visual tour. Readers get the Washington of the 1890s in photographs, street by street and building by building.
29253-the-girl-scouts-a-training-school-:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this pamphlet, number 11 in the Girl Scouts series from national headquarters in New York. Wiggin, a beloved children's author, argues that Girl Scouting trains girls for womanhood. She says she was always a Girl Scout herself in spirit, even before the name existed, and that her early story was scouty in tone.

Wiggin recalls educating street children in San Francisco and writing books for younger children, until Polly Oliver's Problem brought her a girl public. From that experience she speaks for scouting as character training. Readers get a short, warm endorsement of the early Girl Scouts by a famous author, valuable as a record of how the movement presented itself to parents.
29681-a-mountain-boyhood:
Joe Mills recalls his boyhood in the mountains in this 1926 memoir, with pictures by Enos B. Comstock. He starts by going west as a boy. Then he learns wild country and its beasts at first hand. A first camp alone, a log cabin in the wilds, trapping, glacier climbs, and forest fires follow. The busy work of beavers gets its own chapter, and bears loom large throughout.

Later chapters cross the Divide, seek gold, and end in Rocky Mountain National Park. Mills writes in a plain, warm voice. The book reads as a boy's own record of hard days, close calls, and the slow craft of living outdoors. It suits young readers who like true tales of the high country.
29969-the-celtic-magazine-vol-1-no-3-jan:
The Celtic Magazine, number three, is dated January 1876. Its leading piece continues The State of the Ossianic Controversy. Mr. Arnold's handsome but slightly ambiguous admission, the writer says, is that the Celts, intellectually, approach the secrets of nature and its magic closely. In reality, that points to a keener feeling for certain natural affinities than do their Anglo-Saxon brethren.

On this reading, Celts grasp more surely when, where, and how physical nature stamps its truest impress on the soul's percipient faculties. Such intuitions give them a kind of inspiration, or second-sight of nature, like prophecy, that lends their highest poetic utterance a rapt enthusiasm. Reading Ossian from Macpherson's text, however, demands more: a purely scientific insight into nature's hidden powers and an augury of her possible future development.
30322-the-helpful-hand-of-god:
Tom Godwin tells The Helpful Hand of God in Analog, December 1961, with pictures by Barberis. The helpful hand of God, the tagline says, can be very helpful indeed, though it has long been known that God helps those who wisely help themselves. A Vogarian Revised Encyclopedia entry explains that Golden Saints, Yellow Saints, is a term of contempt. The Vogarian State Press applied it to members of the Church of the Golden Rule.

Those members opposed the war then planned against Alkoria. The church, called fanatics resisting state control and advocating social chaos through individual freedom, was liquidated in the Unity Purge. Two thousand of the more able drew sentences to Belen Nine's moon mines. The prison ship never arrived, and the condemned Saints are assumed to have overpowered the guards and escaped to some section of the galaxy. Kane watches Commander Y'Nor glare at a chronometer.
30900-the-tyranny-of-god:
Joseph Lewis wrote this book on the philosophy of atheism, published by the Freethought Press Association in New York with a 1921 copyright. Lewis dedicates it to Fay, his dear wife and comrade. A special edition of two hundred and fifty copies, on Utopian paper in limp leather with gilt top, was autographed and numbered by the author. New editions followed in 1921, 1922, 1928, 1930, 1939, and 1943.

Clarence Darrow, the noted lawyer and philosopher, praised the book in a printed endorsement as a clear, bold, and true statement, plain as a multiplication table. Lewis argues against the rule of God as tyranny, in plain, forceful prose meant for general readers. It remains a classic of American freethought, best read as a document of its time and of the atheist movement that kept it in print for two decades.
31868-red-riding-hood:
This illustrated Red Riding Hood, entered for copyright in 1863 by L. Prang and Company of Massachusetts, retells the familiar tale in verse for children. It opens in a lonely cabin within a dark, old wood, where Red Riding Hood dwells with her mother beneath tall old trees that supply their winter fire.

A rippling brook brings water from far-off mountains, squirrels hoard nuts in hollow trees, and bees make pounds of sweetest honey for the household. Readers get a mid-nineteenth-century picture book, gentle and moral, in which a good and loving girl, kind in daily acts, walks the wood that every child reader knows to fear.
32115-rose-macleod:
Alice Brown's Rose Macleod, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap in April 1908, opens in a Georgian house in early spring. Madam Fulton and her granddaughter Electra sit at the breakfast table on a warm, inspiriting day, while the garden under the dining-room windows tells the season like a floral clock. The earliest blossoms have been pushed onward, and the firstlings of May are budding.

The house itself, mellow with time, stands in abundant acreage. A terraced garden lies to the rear, another garden run wild on the west, and an orchard reaching into level fields and pine groves. Three unshaded dining-room windows give a large outlook on that beauty. Readers get a novel of New England domestic life, opening in a household where grandmother, granddaughter, and the coming spring set the scene.
33019-the-green-god:
Frederic Arnold Kummer's Green God, published in New York in 1911 and illustrated by R. F. Schabelitz, is a mystery of a missing woman and an Eastern idol. Its chapters run from Mr. Ashton and a cry in the morning, through a queer discovery and advice to Miss Temple, to Major Temple's story, an Oriental perfume, and a temple of Buddha. An inspector's conclusions and Miss Temple's testimony carry the plot to a night of horror and the secret of the green room.

The frontispiece shows a frightened man announcing that Miss Temple cannot be found, and that disappearance drives the tale. Kummer mixes detective work with exotic menace, in the manner of popular thrillers of the period. The novel moves from an October afternoon walk toward Exeter into a world of temples, perfumes, and revenge, and it rewards readers who enjoy a mystery with a touch of the uncanny.
33042-hastings-and-neighbourhood:
Walter Higgins's Hastings and Neighbourhood presents the Sussex coast town and its surroundings in words and pictures. It was described by Higgins and painted by E. W. Haslehust for Blackie's Beautiful England series in 1920. A frontispiece shows the old town. A few old timbered houses and two churches, one on each side of the slope, stand with the castle as the sum of tangible reminders of ancient days. The book belongs to a series that also covered Bath, Canterbury, the Cornish Riviera, Dartmoor, and the English Lakes.

Higgins walks readers through streets, castle, and coast, while Haslehust's paintings give color to the scenes. The guide suits travelers who wanted beauty with history, and it preserves Hastings as it looked just after the First World War. For lovers of English towns and illustrated travel books, it is a pleasant, well-pictured introduction to a famous seaside place.
33626-the-career-of-leonard-wood:
Joseph Hamblen Sears traces the career of General Leonard Wood in this 1920 biography, copyrighted in 1919. A prefatory poem by Corinne Roosevelt Robinson, dated November 11, 1918, hails Wood as a great-visioned soul whose leadership kept ardent youth from faltering. Ten chapters follow the subject through Indian fighter, official, soldier, organizer, administrator, statesman, patriot, the Great War, and the result.

Sears writes in the days immediately following the Great War, when Wood stood as a prominent public figure and presidential possibility. The biography balances military service with civil administration and political ambition, presenting Wood as a man of vision and energy. Readers of American military and political history will find a contemporary, admiring portrait from the height of Wood's reputation.
34186-the-copeland-method:
Vanness Copeland of Buffalo, New York, wrote this complete manual for cleaning, repairing, altering, and pressing all kinds of garments for men and women, at home or for business, copyrighted in 1908. An index runs from equipment and tools through formulas for cleaning fluid and moth preventative to removing stains, darning a three-cornered tear, alterations, and pressing.

Later sections treat cutaway, Prince Albert, military, and other uniforms, ladies' jackets, selection of materials, care of clothes, folding, testing goods, a price list, how to dress, and business etiquette. Copeland holds that neatness needs only ordinary care, and first impressions last. The manual offers a practical tailor's guide.
34479-the-history-of-painting-in-italy-v:
The History of Painting in Italy is the English form of the great Italian art history by the Abate Luigi Lanzi. Thomas Roscoe translated it, and Simpkin and Marshall published it in London in 1828, in six volumes. Its span runs from the revival of the fine arts to the end of the eighteenth century.

The first volume contains the schools of Florence and Siena. Lanzi organized Italian painting by regional schools, a scheme that shaped art history for a century. Roscoe's advertisement declines to add explanation to the author's own preface. He offers only acknowledgment of those who helped the translation. For English readers Lanzi was the gateway to the Italian primitives and masters alike. The work's school by school method still underlies how museums hang Italian pictures.
34585-the-history-of-painting-in-italy-v:
The History of Painting in Italy, by the Abate Luigi Lanzi, traces art from its revival to the end of the seventeen-hundreds. Thomas Roscoe turned the work into English, and this second volume was printed in London in 1828. The full work runs to six volumes.

This volume holds the schools of Rome and Naples, the third and fourth books of the set. The Roman school is cut into five epochs, from the old masters to the age of decline. Raffaello and his school fill the second epoch at great length. The fourth tells how Barocci and others restored the art. The Neapolitan book runs from its old masters to Luca Giordano and Solimene. Lanzi weighs whether Rome even counts as a school of its own.
34645-the-history-of-painting-in-italy-v:
The Abate Luigi Lanzi wrote this tale of the art of paint in Italy, and Thomas Roscoe put it in English dress. The set runs to six books, and this is the third, printed at London in 1828. Its span is from the new birth of the fine arts to the end of the age two past our own. The theme of this book is set on its title leaf: it holds the School of Venice.

The list of parts splits that school in four spans of time. The first span treats of the old masters of the town. The next is the great age: Giorgione, Titian, Tintoretto, Jacopo da Bassano, and Paolo Veronese. The third span treats of the new turns of the men of the age of the manner, and of the rot of the paint of Venice.
36203-neath-the-hoof-of-the-tartar-or-th:
Baron Nicolas Jósika wrote a Hungarian tale of the Tartar storm. Selina Gaye cut and turned it into English. Bain wrote the front words for this second form of 1904. A photo plate of Jósika fronts the book in grave dress. Sans peur et sans reproche is its proud French motto.

Talk of war leads, and good news or bad is the next ask. Master Stephen's page and a first fault fill the first parts. As the king wills and a next fault build the foe's near tread. At the doors, the brave part of valor is weighed in fear. A keep is held, camp fires glow, and a dire day dawns. Dora's vow and a snow road close the arc.
36208-lectures-on-the-true-the-beautiful:
M V Cousin lectures on the true, the beautiful, and the good were rendered into English by O W Wight, with Cousin approval. D Appleton and Company in New York issued the book in eighteen seventy two, from a copyright of eighteen fifty four. An appendix on French art adds to the lectures. Wight gave the book to Sir William Hamilton of Edinburgh, a teacher of logic and metaphysics.

Cousin treats truth, beauty, and goodness as the great heads of thought and life. A line from the Platonists and the Fathers heads the book, that God is the life of the soul as the soul is the life of the body. Wight praises Hamilton for clearing the doctrine of common sense and for a doctrine of the conditioned. Students of philosophy get a famed French voice in clear English dress.
36692-the-whole-armour-of-god:
Whole Armour of God is a book of sermons by Jowett, a famed preacher. The title takes Paul's image of the Christian's full armour from Ephesians. Jowett's My Daily Meditation for the Circling Year stands advertised beside it. Both volumes sold cloth bound at a dollar thirty five net. Transcriber notes list small fixes made page by page in the text.

One page of the original lacks lines, marked as missing text here. The sense of that passage stays clear from its context anyway. Jowett preached to crowded halls in London and in New York. His sermons join plain speech with deep comfort for hard times. Belt, breastplate, shield, and sword of the spirit fill his theme.
37132-songs-of-womanhood:
Songs of Womanhood is a book of verse by Laurence Alma Tadema. It was put out at London in nineteen hundred and three. A note at the front tells the root of the book. A great num ber of its songs were known past this in small sheets. Those sheets did not reach the crowd. So the songs are put in book form here.

Three or four more songs are add from the sheets of the day. A num ber are print here for the first time. The same hand's past book is named at the front. A great sheet is quoted on it in praise. In this book the critic knew with a rush of joy the work of a true bard, that sheet said. A next sheet found deep sense in it, and a thought that sees.
38198-frederica-and-her-guardians-or-the:
Margaret Robertson wrote this tale of an orphan girl and her guardians. Hodder and Stoughton printed this edition in 1881. The Perils of Orphanhood is the book's second title, and its first chapter's name.

The Vanes' house stands in a large, fair garden, walled in high brick. From the street only the waving tops of its trees can be seen. Such houses were built in the country, amid fields and orchards, the tale says. Then the town grew out and shut them in, its hum and bustle close at hand. Frederica's lot in that house, with no parents to shield her, forms the tale's long test of a young heart.
38967-the-history-of-painting-in-italy-v:
Volume four of The History of Painting in Italy, by the Abate Luigi Lanzi, was turned into English by Thomas Roscoe. The London edition of 1828 ran to six volumes in all. This volume contains the schools of Lombardy, Mantua, Modena, Parma, Cremona, and Milan. Its history runs from the revival of the fine arts to the end of the eighteenth century.

The history of painting in upper Italy fills the book’s second part. The Mantuan school opens the chapters of this volume. Lanzi sorted Italian painting by schools and cities, a plan still in use. Roscoe gave English readers that great survey in their own tongue. Painters great and small stand in their local lines here. The volume serves students of the Renaissance and its heirs.
39996-the-history-of-painting-in-italy-v:
The History of Painting in Italy, volume five, was printed in 1828. Simpkin and Marshall published the London translation that year. Thomas Roscoe rendered Lanzi's Italian into English. Six volumes make the whole history. This volume holds four schools of upper Italy. Bologna leads, arranged in epochs. Ancient masters open the school; Francia's age follows. The Caracci and their scholars form the third epoch. Cignani and the Clementine academy close the fourth. Ferrara takes the next book, under the Este dukes. Genoa and Piedmont end the volume.

Epochs divide each school alike: rise, flower, and decline. Lanzi tracks fame as it moves from city to city. Wherever art fixed its seat, he writes, some branch of painting was perfected. The fifth volume is the standard English Lanzi for the north.
402-penrod:
Booth Tarkington follows twelve-year-old Penrod Schofield through a year of school, shows, and scrapes in this comic novel. Penrod, who guards his feelings behind a blank face, hates the pageant his mother forces him to join. His dog Duke, his friends, and the town's grown-ups keep pulling him into fresh trouble.

Chapters track a costume, a smallpox scare, a birthday party, and a feud with a show-off rival. Tarkington writes boyhood with fond humor, catching how a child thinks and hides thought. The book endures as a warm, funny portrait of growing up in a small American town.
41398-generals-of-the-british-army-portr:
Francis Dodd drew color portraits of the chiefs of the British Army in war. The book came out in London in 1917 from the Country Life house. Short life notes go with each drawn face. Haig leads the list as field marshal of the hosts. Plumer, Rawlinson, and Gough come next in rank order.

Allenby, Horne, Birdwood, and Byng fill the mid list. Congreve, who won the realm's top cross for grit, stands there too. Each note gives the man's posts, wars, and awards in brief. Town readers in war time could put faces to famed names. The book is both art and a roll of fame. Fine color work gives it worth past its day.
41533-the-history-of-painting-in-italy-v:
Thomas Roscoe translated The History of Painting in Italy from the Italian of Luigi Lanzi. Simpkin and Marshall published the six volumes in London in 1828. This file holds volume six, which contains the indexes to the whole work. Lanzi's history runs from the revival of the fine arts to the end of the eighteenth century, and this volume is the key that unlocks the other five.

Three indexes divide the labour. The first lists every painter mentioned, with dates of birth and death and the authorities for them. The second gathers the historical and critical books about art that Lanzi cited. The third picks out the most important matters in the work. Entries begin with the Abati family of Modena, giving fathers, sons, and brothers in turn. For students of Italian art the index volume turned Lanzi's narrative into a reference tool, quarried by later writers for a century.
4364-the-lances-of-lynwood:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this historical tale for young readers, drawing on Froissart's chronicle and the old French life of Bertrand du Guesclin. Her preface hopes the sketch may lead young readers to Froissart himself, not put off by how large his books are. Orthon's tale, she notes, follows Froissart almost word for word, and it resembles German and Irish legends.

The Lances of Lynwood follows a young English knight in the chivalric world of the fourteenth century, with its battles, courts, and codes. Yonge tells the tale with her usual moral care, making history into adventure. It remains a good introduction to the age of chivalry for younger readers, and for adults who enjoy it too.
44941-the-government-of-god:
The Government of God is a theological treatise by John Taylor, an apostle of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, published at Liverpool in 1852. Taylor wrote it while presiding over the French and German missions. The preface, by James Linforth, explains that Taylor's mission cares kept him from seeing the book through the press himself.

The chapters set out a Mormon doctrine of divine rule. They treat the object of man's existence, man's accountability to God, and the Lord's course in governing the world. Later chapters ask whose right it is to govern, whether God's kingdom will be literal or spiritual, and what its establishment on earth will bring. The opening chapter defines the kingdom simply: the government of God on earth or in heaven, upholding every planetary system by his power.
45148-pharisaism-its-aim-and-its-method:
Pharisaism: Its Aim and Its Method is a theological study by Herford, issued as volume thirty-five of the Crown Theological Library. The series list at the front shows its company. Harnack, Otto, and Kirsopp Lake stand among its past authors. The library sold short, learned books on the faith at a few shillings each. Herford's subject is the Pharisees of the Gospels. Christian preaching had long made their name a byword for hollow form and pride.

Herford sets out to read them by their own aim and method. What did the Pharisees mean to do for the religion of Israel? By what rules of study and life did they work? The book treats the scribes as builders of a lived faith, not as stock villains. It is a fair-minded piece of the liberal scholarship of its day.
45270-the-seven-ages-of-childhood:
Carolyn Wells wrote verses and Jessie Smith drew pictures for each age of childhood. The book came out in New York in 1909. Seven young friends who posed for the art get a warm thanks. Each part pairs a full picture with a short verse set.

First comes the infant safe in its mother arms at rest. Then come the toddling boy, the young gourmet, and the lover. School days and slim maidenhood lead to the last scene of all. The book turns a famed speech on life stages into child charm.
46011-the-moving-picture-boys-and-the-fl:
Victor Appleton wrote a boys' tale of film boys in a great flood. The book came out in 1914 with Grosset and Dunlap. Its sub-title names dire days on the Mississippi in full. A front plate shows Joe at work as a house drifts past. Appleton wrote the Tom Swift books in those same years.

Joe films the house as it floats down stream in peril. Film work in quake land stands in the set's past books. Flood, wreck, and save acts test the boys' cool heads. Their lens takes all while their hands aid the hurt. Such tales taught boys a new craft through fast plots. The pace stays high from first page to last.
46190-stories-of-robin-hood:
Stories of Robin Hood is a school reader by Bertha Bush, copyrighted in 1912. Owen of Dansville and Hall and McCreary of Chicago published it jointly. It is number 212 of the Instructor Literature Series. Seven tales make up the contents. Winning the sheriff's golden arrow comes first. How Little John joined Robin Hood follows. Allen-a-Dale and Friar Tuck share a chapter.

The sorrowful knight, the king, and the death of Robin Hood close the set. The opening tale starts before Robin's outlawry, with his father's grief. Peter the Ploughman has been hanged for shooting the king's deer. His crops had been trampled by huntsmen and his children cried for hunger. Norman oppression of Saxon commoners frames the boy's indignation. Bush shapes the old ballads for classroom reading.
46948-the-disaster-which-eclipsed-histor:
Richard K Fox published a quick, cheap account of the Johnstown flood. The Disaster Which Eclipsed History sold at ten cents from Franklin Square, New York. Rights rest from 1889 with the publisher. A bold front page cries horror at a death-dealing dam.

The Conemaugh River burst forth on Friday evening, May 31, the tale opens. At four o'clock all was serene; at six, desolation ruled Johnstown. Hundreds upon hundreds were swept away when the big dam broke. The river ran through northwestern Pennsylvania, past homes set along its banks. In quiet times it carried picnickers and moonlight parties on calm water. Readers gain raw, instant journalism from the days just after the flood.
47448-harvey-s-views-on-the-use-of-the-c:
Harvey's Views on the Circulation of the Blood was issued in 1915. Columbia University Press published Curtis's lecture that December. Curtis had taught physiology at Columbia for years. The piece began as a lecture of 1907. The Johns Hopkins Hospital Historical Club heard it at Baltimore. A portrait of Harvey by Jonson fronts the book. It comes from the collected works of 1766. A prefatory note explains the translations. Harvey wrote and published in Latin alone. Willis Englished the works for the Sydenham Society in 1847. Curtis uses Willis in part, with changes of his own. In large part he translates afresh from the Latin.

Each passage is keyed by page and line to both editions. The reader may thus give every quotation its context. Curtis asks what the circulation was for, in Harvey's own view.
48909-the-ashes-of-a-god:
The Ashes of a God, translated by Bain, was first published in London in 1911. Methuen issued the book, with a frontispiece. Its title page claims a rendering from the original manuscript. Verses signed with Hindu names open and close the parts. Three tales make the volume: A Mountain of Merit, A Fetter of the Soul, and The Waves of Time. The first opens with an invocation to the skull-adorned god. Two Brahmans quarrel on the bank of a sacred stream below the Himalaya.

Their dispute turns on rank and family pride. One claims the line of Agastya for his house. Scorn and anger pass between them. Footnotes explain the Sanskrit terms for English readers. Bain writes India as a land of gods, rivers, and pride, in a rich, archaic style.
49953-the-queen-s-maries-a-romance-of-ho:
The Queens Maries is a romance of Holyrood by Whyte Melville, author of a shelf of tales of sport, war, and high life. This form is a new issue from a London house, with a word of gift at its front. That word makes the book out to a lady whose work in the past had done much for the fame of a slurred queen.

An old Scots ballad heads the first part. Last night the queen had four Maries, it sings. Today she will have but three. The names of the four maids of Mary Stuart are told in the song. The tale then opens in the court of that queen, with love, plot, and the doom that hangs on her house.
5080-magnum-bonum-or-mother-carey-s-broo:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Magnum Bonum, or Mother Carey's Brood, opens with Joe Brownlow's fancy and a plea for a little teacher at Miss Heath's school. The girl has had measles last and worst, came from an asylum for officers' daughters, and has no home at all, while the house must be purified and its people go away.

She cannot travel with them, since their sister has children, and would otherwise roam from room to room before the whitewashers, in a critical state of chest. Mother Carey takes her in, and the brood's story follows. Readers get a domestic novel of kindness and family life, where a holiday guest becomes part of the household's heart.
50957-man-and-the-glacial-period:
Man and the Glacial Period treats the ice age and the first traces of human life within it. The book belongs to the International Scientific Series, a set of one volume works by leading men of science. A long list at the front names the series, from Tyndall on glaciers to Spencer on society. Each volume sold bound in cloth at a set price.

The series aimed to put sound science before general readers. Its list runs through physics, chemistry, mind, law, and the descent of man. This volume asks how old mankind is beside the great ice sheets. River gravels, caves, and buried tools supply the proof its age debated. The question stood near the centre of Victorian science. Such series volumes carried the debate into homes and libraries.
51037-second-childhood:
Second Childhood, a science fiction story by Clifford D Simak, ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in February 1951. Its world has won immortality for all, and made it inescapable. No normal way to die remains. Men live with wild care and hope for a lucky accident to kill them, and still they live on.

Andrew Young comes before the immortality commission with a strange plea. He asks leave to discontinue his life. Since suicide has been made impossible to the mind, he asks the board to name next friends to arrange his end. The chairman calls the plea irregular and without precedent. Young answers that the commission exists to work out the kinks in immortality, and that his case is one of the kinks.
51499-blueblood:
Blueblood is a short star tale by Jim Harmon from the December nineteen sixty Galaxy. A ship crew first sees the folk of a new world in two shades of blue. Four dark Indigo men bear a light Azure man in a chair seat. The ship pilot tells the tale and grants the two lore men outrank him. Lee Chon reads the chair as a priest seat at first glance in the talk.

Mike Ellik doubts that, since the chair lacks rich dress marks of rank. Three bear men look slow of mind to the lore eyes at first sight. The fourth bears a slack face he could change at will, they note. The chair man shows no mind harm in his clear strong form. Breed slave stock is one guess the two lore men trade in talk.
51943-the-golden-flood:
The Golden Flood is a Wall Street novel by Edwin Lefevre, published by McClure, Phillips at New York in 1905, with pictures by Leigh. It is dedicated to Daniel Gray Reid. Part One, The Flood, opens in a bank president's office. He studies the underwriters' plan of the latest industrial merger: capital stock of one hundred million dollars, assets for publication the same, the lawyers calling it fully legal.

A gentleman seeks to deposit one hundred thousand dollars, with a letter of introduction to the president. His card names George Kitchell Grinell, a name the president has never heard. The stranger is young, square-shouldered, and careful in dress, with gold-rimmed glasses giving him a student's air. Money and mystery meet in the opening scene.
52655-the-ornithosauria-an-elementary-st:
Harry Seeley made this elementary study of pterodactyle bones at Cambridge. Deighton, Bell printed The Ornithosauria in 1870 with twelve plates. The bones came from fossil remains in the Cambridge Upper Greensand. They stand arranged in the Woodwardian Museum of the university there.

The preface says Professor Sedgwick asked for a catalogue of the museum. Indexes, memoirs, and species accounts divide the planned work in three. The university press syndics paid the printing cost of the volume. It forms one part of the catalogue, made for students use. Sedgwick thanks in print stand in the front matter for the syndics great favour shown.
54121-tom-pinder-foundling-a-story-of-th:
Tom Pinder, Foundling is a penny story by Sykes, printed at Slaithwaite by Walker at the Britannia Works. Its subtitle calls it a story of the Holmfirth flood. Sykes was a solicitor, scholar, and newspaper owner of the Colne Valley. The tale later came out under the title Dorothy’s Choice.

Sykes traced his own roots to Holme village above Slaithwaite in pride. His grandsire was a clothier, and the woollen trade fed his fiction. The Holmfirth flood of his tale was a real drowning disaster of the valley. A foundling hero carries the village story through its waters. Penny tales of local disaster sold by the thousand in such towns. This one keeps a Yorkshire flood in living memory.
54579-the-stolen-aeroplane-or-how-bud-wi:
The Stolen Aeroplane, or How Bud Wilson Made Good, is a boys' novel by Ashton Lamar, printed at Chicago in 1910. It is the second book of the Aeroplane Boys series. The publishers promise that these stories are the newest and most up-to-date, and that all aeroplane details are correct.

Doug Jackson, driver of the Scottsville House bus, rises from the edge of the depot platform as the story gets under way. All are waiting for passenger train number twenty-two, west bound, due at a quarter past eleven and late as usual. The frontispiece cries: Stop, in the name of the law. The series began with In the Clouds for Uncle Sam and went on to The Boy Aviator's Grit. A companion Airship Boys series by H L Sayler is advertised at the front.
55161-the-madness-of-philip-and-other-ta:
The Madness of Philip and Other Tales of Childhood is a set of short stories by Josephine Dodge Daskam, printed at New York in 1902. Cory drew the pictures, and Daskam gave the book to her father, the kindest of her many critics. Seven tales fill the contents, from the title story to Edgar, the Choir Boy Uncelestial.

Philip's madness opens before breakfast, with the boy trying to stuff his sister into a bolster case, muffling her cries with a pillow. His hidden rubbers keep the school bus waiting, and the jolted children reach kindergarten ready for a fight, which Philip duly provides. Daskam writes of children with a sharp eye and no syrup, catching their wars and prides exactly.
55222-misunderstood:
Misunderstood is a tale of child life by Florence Montgomery. The author states up front that the book is not a childs own story. It is meant for grown folk who care to see life as a child sees it. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

The preface asks readers to stoop to a childs small hopes and hurts. It says the inner life of the young is too oft missed or misread. Small joys and trials that fill a childs day form its whole sum. The tale then shows those small things from the childs own eye line. Its plea for soft sight of the young made the book a long loved work.
55730-joe-wayring-at-home-or-the-adventu:
Joe Wayring at Home, or the Adventures of a Fly Rod, is a boys' book. Harry Castlemon wrote it for the Forest and Stream Series of tales. Winston of Philadelphia, Chicago, and Toronto published the volume for boys. A front plate shows the battle with the squatters in bold action. Castlemon's Gunboat, Rocky Mountain, and Sportsman Club series front the book.

Frank the Young Naturalist heads the six Gunboat volumes in that list. Frank in the Woods and Frank on a Gunboat follow in order. Rocky Mountain tales send Frank among rancheros and into high peaks. The Sportsman Club rides, floats, and traps through its three volumes. Joe Wayring's rod and stream promise the same outdoor sport at home.
564-the-mystery-of-edwin-drood:
Charles Dickens left his last novel unfinished at his death, and the mystery of Edwin Drood has puzzled readers ever since. Young Drood vanishes from Cloisterham, a cathedral town of deans, nuns, and opium dreams. Dickens died in 1870 with only half the novel written, leaving six monthly parts done.

Chapters follow John Jasper, Rosa Bud, and Neville Landless through suspicion, a night with Durdles, and a flight, but no ending survives. The book fascinates as much for what Dickens never wrote as for the rich, dark story he did. Readers have offered endings ever since, from stage plays to new novels that finish the tale.
56736-chronicles-of-chicora-wood:
Chronicles of Chicora Wood is a house past book by Elizabeth Allston Pringle. A Scribner house of New York brought it out in May of nineteen twenty two. Pringle wrote A Woman Rice Planter in a past book of like ground. A front photo shows her at Chicora Wood in this print at start. Part one, My Father, heads the five part scheme of the book.

Heads there trace the two L Allstons rise and a sire as planter and town man. Part two turns to her dam, old field school, and match days in rank. Part three tells her own tale: babe woes, small school house, and sea warm months. War times fill part four with a match, a safe house, and grief ranks. Heads there brace to meet Sherman and walk his host track in the scheme.
56873-psychology-and-parenthood:
Addington Bruce wrote Psychology and Parenthood, for Dodd, Mead in 1919. Rights were held in 1915, and the book is given to his sister. Bruce had written The Riddle of Personality and works on mental healing. Contents open with the importance of the environment in a child's life. Suggestion in education takes the second chapter of the book.

The secret of genius and intensive child culture follow in the list. The problem of laziness and a chapter on laughter come next. Hysteria in childhood and the menace of fear close the course. Chapter one opens with a story of two small boys on a country road. An orchard in autumn glory tempts them over the fence and up a tree. The owner comes from a near cottage, and down they scramble. Bruce builds his counsel for parents on such small scenes.
57372-the-literary-history-of-the-adelph:
Austin Brereton wrote a history of the Adelphi, a small district of streets and terraces just west of the Strand in London. The first edition came out in 1907, and the edition shown here was printed in New York in 1909. Brereton tells the story of the ground itself and of the well known men and women who lived there.

Inside, the book moves house by house and street by street in plain story form. It names residents such as Vicesimus Knox, the maker of the book Elegant Extracts, who lived at No. 1, Adam Street. Prints and views of the old streets fill the book. Brereton wrote for the general reader as well as for lovers of old London, and he took care to get the small facts right.
5773-annals-of-a-quiet-neighbourhood:
George MacDonald narrates Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood through a clergyman newly arrived at Marshmallows. Chapters follow despondency and consolation, a first Sunday and Monday, a coffin, visitors from the hall, Oldcastle Hall, the bishop's basin, and what the narrator preached. An organist, a Christmas party, a sermon on God and Mammon, and pupils like young Weir fill the parish year.

This gives a gentle chronicle of village life, where sermons, visits, and small kindnesses matter more than great events. MacDonald's moral imagination softens doctrine into story, letting parishioners teach the parson as much as he teaches them. The book suits readers who enjoy Victorian clerical fiction, quiet humor, and a portrait of community built one Sunday at a time.
58122-a-guide-to-cromer-and-its-neighbou:
A Guide to Cromer and Its Neighbourhood tells of a town on the sea. The writer gives no name, and calls the self a mere guest there. The book came out in towns of that coast in the year 1841. Verse at the front sings of waves, cliffs, and woods of the place.

The first words own the guide had long been felt as a want. The writer claims no fresh finds and no fault free work in it. A few free hours gave the chance to fill the gap for guests. Thanks go to those whose facts built the book in large part. Health in the air, an open sea, and fine views are its boasts. The ill, the bookish, and the wild at heart all gain from its shore. Why the town is not more known is a muse of the first page.
58593-the-garden-of-god:
Garden of God is a South Seas novel by Stacpoole of Ireland. Dodd, Mead published it in New York with rights in 1923. Stacpoole had written The Blue Lagoon, and this tale returns there.
