Contents divide it into two books: On the Island, The Children Return. Book one opens with The Cormorant, Dawn, and The Vision in turn.

Dick Em, the title chapter, and Here Once They Dwelt follow there. The keeper of the lagoon, sunset, and the rollers close book one. Book two opens as time passes and the children return home. A first glimpse of the demon and Katafa darken the island idyll. Blown to sea, a fire on the reef, and a fight ensue.
58744-money-is-the-root-of-all-good:
Patrick Wilkins wrote a tale of a crash on a world where good deeds are cash. The tale ran in Worlds of If in October 1954. Class AA call for Universal Relief heads the wild news. The stock mart has crashed on the world Lyrane, it says. There folk live by a trade built on good deeds in sum.

No cause is known, and star cheats who water stock are eyed. Kalgor, crown town of the vast realm, starts the tale's view. That town is more farm and suburb than one dense pile, it notes. Realm rule and realm trade sprawl through all the stars. Their top cream sits in small homes on green Kalgor. Wit and coin mix.
58985-the-babees-book-medieval-manners-f:
Edith Rickert turned these medieval courtesy texts into modern English from the texts edited by Furnivall. Chatto and Windus at London, with Duffield at New York, published the book in 1908 in the New Medieval Library. Manuscript pictures illustrate it, from the School of Aristotle as frontispiece to a civic deputation received by John of Gaunt.

The Babees Book opens the collection, a report of how young people should behave, praying that tender years may learn courtesy and virtue from it. Around it stand The ABC of Aristotle, Urbanitatis, The Little Children's Little Book, and Stans Puer ad Mensam, on standing at table. How the Good Wife Taught Her Daughter and How the Wise Man Taught His Son stand with them. John Russell's Book of Nurture, The Book of Courtesy, and the schools of virtue by Hugh Rhodes, Francis Seager, and Richard Weste follow, with notes at the end.
59009-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The hosted text is an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Mrs Henry Wood, the Victorian novelist, compiled by David Widger. It is not a novel but a guide. It lists every one of her books held by the library, and prints the table of contents of each.

East Lynne stands first, her most famous tale. The contents of that book name Lady Isabel, Barbara Hare, and Mr Carlyle's office. The broken cross, the moonlight interview, and the keepers of the dead fill the chapter heads. The Channings, Verner's Pride, and Elster's Folly follow. The six series of Johnny Ludlow tales are listed in order. The Shadow of Ashlydyat closes the main list. The index serves readers who wish to find their way into a long shelf of sensation novels.
59633-history-of-the-harvard-college-obs:
History of the Harvard College Observatory covers the years eighteen forty to eighteen ninety, by Daniel Baker. It was first printed as six Saturday pieces in a Boston newspaper. Edward Pickering, the observatory's director, wrote the preface to this pamphlet form. The Cambridge printing is dated eighteen ninety, the fiftieth year of the institution.

The first recorded sighting at the observatory fell on the last day of eighteen thirty nine. The first director's appointment followed in February eighteen forty, with overseers confirming later. Baker writes for the general public, not for men of the science alone. He traces how Harvard kept in the front rank of the star science. New facts from early records were dug out for the first time here. Pictures on one page show the instruments and buildings of the place.
59767-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of William Wood is a finding aid compiled by David Widger. William Wood was a Canadian historian of war and empire. His books, many written as chronicles for a popular series, fill the index with battles on land and sea.

Captains of the Civil War leads the contents, a chronicle of the blue and the gray. The Great Fortress chronicles Louisbourg from 1720 to 1760. The Passing of New France and The Winning of Canada treat the fall of French Canada. The Father of British Canada follows Governor Carleton. Elizabethan Sea Dogs, The War with the United States, Flag and Fleet, and All Afloat complete the list. For each work the index prints the full table of contents. It is a reader's map to a national historian's whole shelf, in one plain file.
5986-clara-hopgood:
Mark Rutherford sets his tale ten miles northeast of Eastthorpe, in Fenmarket, a town wholly in the Fens. Its roads run level, monotonous, and straight, flanked by deep stagnant ditches, and its river moves broader and slower toward the sea. The flat country shapes the story's mood.

Clara and Madge Hopgood, two young women playing chess in their mother's back parlor on a dark November afternoon in 1844, anchor the opening. Rutherford writes plainly about provincial life, family duty, and conscience. The novel follows sisters whose quiet choices carry real moral weight.
59974-handicaps-of-childhood:
Handicaps of Childhood is a study of child troubles by Addington Bruce. Dodd, Mead of New York brought the book out in the year 1921. Bruce held the rights from 1917 and gives it to his father. He had writ Psychology and Parenthood and The Riddle of Personality. Ten chapters run from mental backwardness to night terrors at the end.

The only child, the child who sulks, and jealousy fill the next chapters. Selfishness and bashfulness with indecision get chapters of their own here. Stammering and fairy tales that handicap stand in the later list. A distinguished French psychologist opens the first chapter in a Paris school. Doctor Alfred Binet watched a class of forty children at work. A bright-seeming boy of twelve sat among the little ones there. Binet called him backward, not bright, to the principal's shame.
60004-the-fables-of-sop-and-others-with-:
Thomas Bewick's Fables of Aesop, and Others, with designs on wood, was printed by Walker at Newcastle in 1818 for Bewick and Son. A prefatory address to the youth of the British Isles sets out the plan. The publishers gathered the prudential maxims of the ancient sages, and made the pictures worthy of study so the precepts would impress more forcibly. Men drawn as lions, tigers, wolves, and foxes are no extravagant fiction, the preface argues: the young will meet such dispositions in the world.

A facsimile bill heads the volume: an imperial copy at one pound eleven shillings and sixpence, received with thanks by Thomas and Robert Elliot Bewick. The contents table runs alphabetically rather than by page. Bewick's wood engravings made the book famous, and the fables carry the moralising preface's programme of truth, integrity, and honour sown early.
60819-the-lathe-its-uses-or-instruction-:
A thick guide teaches the lathe and the art of turn in wood and steel. The book came out in New York in 1868. A plate shows a first class five inch lathe by Munro of Lambeth. That lathe bears a shaft that rides and gear on high. New tools for grace work on flat and curved faces fill its scope.

Chucks and hand turn in wood lead the list of parts. Hollow work and screw cuts take their due turns in line. The Yankee scroll chuck and steel turn by hand come next. Self fed screw lathes and wheel cuts fill the mid parts. Spheres, fret saws, and slide rests close the long list. A new rose lathe fills the back. Craft men prize it.
61799-the-ecclesiastical-orders-of-knigh:
James van Der Veldt wrote The Ecclesiastical Orders of Knighthood. The Catholic University of America Press issued it in 1956. The study first ran in a church review. Parts ran from October 1955 to January 1956. Three printings followed within two years. Four parts divide the text.

Part One gives the background of knightly orders. Part Two treats the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem. The Teutonic Knights share that part. Iberian orders and the Holy Sepulchre order fill Part Three. Papal orders fill Part Four in full. The Supreme Order of Christ leads them there. The Golden Spur, Pius, Gregory, and Sylvester orders follow. The term covers orders tied to the Church, he opens. Two groups hold them now, he notes. A priest-scholar's survey maps honors that join faith, rank, and old crusade roots.
62175-studies-of-childhood:
James Sully wrote these studies of childhood minds and their ways. Appleton printed the book in New York in 1896. Sully taught mind philosophy and logic at University College, London. His preface owns the studies form no full child psychology treatise.

They treat only sides of child minds that caught his own notice. He aims at exactness with a manner to draw parents and teachers. Part first ran in the Fortnightly Review of November 1895. Extracts from a father diary form part of the later pages. Parts ran in the Popular Science Monthly of New York before the book form came out.
62876-doing-good:
Doing Good is a farthing story book for children, issued by Dean and Son of London. It belongs to Dean Illustrated Farthing Books, a cheap line for young readers. Little Alice wakes one bright May morning as the sun peers through her curtains. A simple morning prayer from her happy heart starts her day of kindness.

Dew sparkles on the earth and birds sing in the apple trees as she looks out. A speckled hen bustles over ten chickens hunting worms and slugs for breakfast. The big Shanghai rooster blasts from his stone like a clarion over the yard. Alice laughter sets the warm tone for the small good deeds that follow.
62877-the-little-princess-in-the-wood:
Sibylle von Olfers made a picture book of a small princess in the wood. Helen Dean Fish wrote the words that go with the plates. The book came out in New York in 1931. Olfers is known for When the Root Children Wake Up. Her soft drawn world suits the very young well.

Princess Rosemary wakes on a fine summer morn and dons her crown. Through the rose tree she spies the Dew Children at play. Rainbow, Glisten, Diamond, Dewdrop, Sparkle, and Pearl call her down. She slips out like a bird to join their games. A clear brook in the meadow is their first stop. Small readers get sun, dew, and gentle fun.
63067-the-story-hour-vol-i-no-1-november:
The Story Hour began with this number, volume one, number one, dated November 1908. The monthly magazine, printed ten times a year at Washington, served story tellers with methods and materials. William C Ruediger of George Washington University edited it. Richard T Wyche, head of the National Story Tellers' League, advised, and Mersene E Sloane founded and published it.

A year cost one dollar in advance, and a single number cost fifteen cents. The league's officers and a board of school and college names fill the front pages. The magazine sought tales for telling and papers on the craft. It marks the moment when story telling in schools and libraries became a trained, shared trade.
63573-trust-in-god:
Trust in God is a small farthing book from Dean and Son at Ludgate Hill in London, in Deans Illustrated Farthing Books. A mother and child talk through a Bible verse in plain words. The verse is Preserve me, O God, for in thee do I put my trust. The mother asks what the psalmist meant by those words.

She recalls a small girl seen walking with her father in the woods last week. At a narrow bridge of two planks with no railing, the girl feared a fall. She asked her father to hold her hand and said she felt no fear when he did. The mother says David felt just so in his time of trouble. He looked up to God as the girl looked up to her father. Young readers get faith taught by a homely, warm tale.
64006-rogers-directory-of-norwich-and-ne:
Rogers' Directory of Norwich and Neighbourhood was printed by Jarrold and Sons at Norwich, from an edition of about 1858. Its preface owns a fault at the start: the work should have come out sooner. A new Guide to Streets was the chief cause of the delay. The compiler found that guide and directory must be made apart, each on its own rounds. In some yards, courts, and back streets, no one could name his own place.

In spite of that, the task was done at last, with great care to shun errors. Norwich is set out as a city and county town in the heart of Norfolk. It held thirty-five parishes and ten hamlets, and spread past six thousand acres. The book lists streets, trades, and homes for folk who needed to find their way and each other.
6469-queen-victoria-her-girlhood-and-wom:
Grace Greenwood writes Queen Victoria's girlhood and womanhood, dedicating the life to Camilla Toulmin, Mrs. Newton Crosland, in memory of a dear old time when the world seemed brighter. Greenwood insists Victoria's life cannot be told without a prefacing sketch of her cousin, Princess Charlotte, who would have been queen had she lived. Charlotte, lovely miracle flower of a loveless marriage, bloomed into noble womanhood amid a corrupt court's petty strifes.

Her happy girlhood, marriage to Prince Leopold, beautiful life at Claremont, and sad death prepared the way, Greenwood argues, for the fair young kinswoman who reigned twenty one years later. A mid passage admires a Sully portrait: no rigidity, no irksome state, only springy, exultant vitality and the dewy morning of life. The princeliness of youth outshines the crown she wears.
65559-the-jade-god:
Alan Sullivan wrote The Jade God, a novel of mystery issued by the Century Company in 1925. The tale opens in an old oak paneled house, where Mr Jarrad and Mr Dawkins take stock of the rooms for their work. A bowl, a clock, and small worn goods are noted one by one in dry, close detail.

Fourteen parts bring in a man from the East, a girl named Jean, a paper knife, and a strange peddler. The jade god of the title hangs over the house as a power some fear and some crave. Night scenes, a flight, a confession, and a broken tile build to the close.
66050-dirty-work-for-doughgod:
Tuttle, a famed hand at western tales, set this yarn in his town of Paradise. Dirty Work for Doughgod opens in full talk, with Mike Pelly laying down the law. No more female teachers for Paradise, he says, and his reason is plain.

All the fool punchers fall in love with her, Mike holds, and her teaching powers go to ruin. This new miss writes from Great Falls, says Doughgod Smith, and she slings a good hand. Let her sling it in Great Falls, says Mike. Whittaker of the Cross J backs him: women have been the bane of his life. Chuck Warner and the tale's teller listen from the saloon steps. Tuttle's dry talk does the rest.
66940-in-a-yellow-wood:
In a Yellow Wood is a novel by Gore Vidal, published in New York in 1947. Dutton issued the first edition. The book is dedicated to Anais Nin. Its title and motto come from a Frost poem. Two roads diverged in a yellow wood, the motto runs. The contents fall into three parts named Day, Night, and The Yellow Wood. Fourteen chapters fill those parts.

The hero is Robert Holton, a young man back from war. The first scene finds him at his mirror at dawn. He checks his hairline for signs of loss. Vidal wrote the novel while still very young. It was his second book, after Williwaw. The tale weighs a veteran's choice of a life path. Office work and old loves pull at him. The Frost lines frame that choice of roads.
67267-thomas-heywood:
Thomas Heywood is a volume of plays in the Mermaid Series, a set of the best plays of the old dramatists. It was edited by A. Wilson Verity, with an opening essay by J. Addington Symonds. The book came out in London in 1888 from Vizetelly and Company, as an unexpurgated edition. A front picture shows the inside of the Red Bull playhouse.

Two verses stand at the front. Beaumont's lines to Ben Jonson recall the Mermaid tavern and its days of swift, flaming wit. Another verse asks what Elysium the souls of dead poets have known. The volume thus sets Heywood among the old English dramatists whose works the series aimed to keep in print, in full form, for the readers of its day.
68080-incidents-of-childhood:
An unnamed writer made this book of tales for children, printed in London in 1821 by B J Holdsworth and by G and W B Whitaker. The Tinner's Son names the lead tale on the title page. A plate called The Two Tempers shows a cart in a ditch. The preface lays down strict rules for tales meant for the young.

Stories should stay familiar in subject and style, slight in build, and stir only light feeling. High drama, the writer warns, can harm children of lively fancy. Books should tempt children to some amusement, never a large share, beside active sports. One tale opens on Peter Simons, a poor fisherman's son in a stone cottage on a cliff two hundred feet over the sea.
68529-firegod:
Firegod is a science fiction story by William Scarff, from Rocket Stories of July nineteen fifty three. Its headnote says Merssu wanted to be a god, not a ruler of systems. A million years and a little luck are all he claims to need. The tale opens as his prime minister bursts in with bad news.

Earthmen are driving past the Rim into the heart of Merssu's empire unchecked. Their ships win battle after battle, and the people mutter of revolt below. Garrisons rise, and the cry goes up that the false emperor must fall. Merssu, once a rebel himself, stays calm and orders a soothing broadcast. Secret weapons, he lies, stand ready if the hour grows truly grave. Then he slips through a hidden door to a private tube way.
69333-1812-a-tale-of-cape-cod:
Michael Fitzgerald wrote a tale of Cape Cod in the War of 1812. The book came out at Yarmouthport in 1912. He gave it to Thacher, a loyal son of the Cape. His front note claims a true view of those hard days. British war ships' guns hung over the Cape's towns then, he says.

Eastham's plight was that of each town on that shore. Sea folk stood bare to the foe, and all trade stood still. State and land chiefs left them to their own grit, he holds. They fought the foe to his boats at times with success. At times they won by wit where arms would fail. Cape folk get their war in home words.
69955-was-it-a-ghost-the-murders-in-buss:
Was It a Ghost? The Murders in Bussey's Wood was published at Boston in 1868. Loring issued the tale at 75 cents. Its title page calls it an extraordinary narrative. A picture named The Ghost stands in the front. The dedication praises a philosophy that can argue without anger. It can hold disbelief, the writer says, without backing it by insolence. Pages of the publisher's fiction lists come first. Alcott's Moods and Alger's tales for boys stand among the adverts.

The narrative itself turns on killings in a wood and a haunting question. Was the power behind the events human, or something more? Cheap Boston fiction of the day loved such riddles. The pamphlet novel dresses a local horror in the dress of a ghost story, and lets the reader judge.
7011-the-flood:
Emile Zola's Flood speaks through Louis Roubien, seventy years old, born at Saint Jory some miles up the Garonne from Toulouse. For fourteen years he battled the earth for daily bread, until prosperity smiled and he stood last month the richest farmer in the parish. His house seemed blessed, happiness reigned, the sun was a brother, and no bad crop could be recalled.

Almost a dozen lived on the farm: Louis himself still hale, his brother Pierre the retired sergeant and old bachelor, and his sister Agathe, commanding, enormous, and gay. His son Jacques, wife Rosie, and their three daughters Aimee, Veronique, and Marie complete the household, with Aimee married to big jolly Cyprica Bouisson. The flood that gives the tale its name will break this peace.
7051-the-good-news-of-god:
Charles Kingsley preaches the good news of God in this 1887 Macmillan collection, transferred from Longman and reprinted many times since 1863. The contents open with the beatific vision, the glory of the cross, and the life of God, then the song of the three children and the eternal goodness. Worship, God's inheritance, De Profundis, and the love of God as its own reward follow.

Later sermons treat the race of life, self respect and self righteousness, true repentance, and the letter and the spirit. Heroes and heroines, the measure of the cross, the pure in heart, music, and the Christ child lead toward Christ's boyhood and the locust swarms. Kingsley preaches a warm, earnest gospel for ordinary hearers.
71701-repton-and-its-neighbourhood:
Hipkins wrote this guide to Repton and its neighbourhood antiquities. Lawrence printed the second edition at Repton in 1899 with photogravures. Hipkins taught as assistant master at Repton School at the time. A first short history of 1892 sold quick, his preface says.

Church, priory, and school centre all that interests in the village. Mercia conversion by Bishop Diuma stands among the famed events here. Danes came in 874 and destroyed abbey and town, he recounts. The priory founding under Peada or Wulphere follows in the guide. Repton Church first building likely dates to Edgar the Peaceable reign, he writes here.
72092-and-it-was-good:
A Earley wrote a tale of a second chance for man and for his maker. And It Was Good ran in Amazing Stories in February 1962, with pictures by Adkins. A carpenter carves wood in anxious moments, shaping faces or fruit trees. His mother brings word that a hard deed has been decided.

Spring comes late: trees stand bare in mid-May with no shoot or bud. Papers recall late snows of 1569 and 1782, yet this year feels wrong. Experts blame radiation from nuclear tests for the halted growth. Readers gain a quiet, strange fable of guilt, mercy, and renewal.
72299-the-party-battles-of-the-jackson-p:
The Party Battles of the Jackson Period, by Claude G Bowers, was first held under a 1922 copyright and later put out in an anniversary printing by Houghton Mifflin. Bowers writes on Andrew Jackson and the fierce party fights of his age. A front print shows Jackson from a painting by Earl.

In his notes Bowers says a fairer view of Jackson has grown with time, yet Jackson stays a source of dispute. He calls Jackson a crusader for key rules of rule by the people, and praises his clean record, hot love of land, and strong American feel. Bowers holds that Jackson was small in small things but great in big ones. Readers get a warm, full case for Jackson and the crowds he led.
7280-my-boyhood:
John Burroughs wrote these sketches of boyhood and early farm life at first in self-defense, because his son Julian had set out to write them and was treading on sacred ground. Burroughs told his son he would be homesick, knowing just how he felt when he left home forty-three years before. He had stayed more or less homesick ever since, with love of old hills and of father and mother deep in his being.

Julian adds a conclusion to his father's sketches, framing a book of farm chores, seasons, and family feeling. Burroughs writes with a naturalist's eye and a son's tenderness, letting small memories carry large affection. The book reads as a return to a lost home, kept alive in prose.
7311-the-leatherwood-god:
William Dean Howells's Leatherwood God draws its historical outline largely from Judge Taneyhill's narrative in the Ohio Valley Series. Its details are often invented, and its characters are invented in their inner growth, though some rest on real persons easy to spot in that narrative. The drama follows the actual events in their main development, as a self-styled god rises among Ohio settlers.

Howells lets the tale test faith, credulity, and frontier hunger for wonder, with an illustration of the towering prophet, hair tossed like a mane, facing his flock. The novel's interest lies less in marvels than in how ordinary people answer them. It stands as a sober American study of false prophecy.
73401-the-wardens-of-cape-cod:
Henry Beston, who later wrote The Outermost House, praised the Coast Guard patrol of Cape Cod in this piece. It ran in The World's Work for December 1923. Two Cape Cods stand in its first lines, set hard against each other.

One Cape is the pictured land of toy windmills, picnics, and motorists. The other is the Cape the sailors see: the wild, houseless outer shore, the countless tragic wrecks, the bars and shoals. That unknown Cape begins at Monomoy, where the silver-gray bones of old wrecks lie in still lagoons. It sweeps on, league upon lonely league, to the hook of Provincetown. The wardens of Beston's title walk that shore by night, watching for ships in peril.
74559-cape-cod:
F. Mitchell wrote this sketch of Cape Cod for The Century Magazine of September 1883. George F. Edwards and Walter J. Fenn drew its cuts. The first cut shows the old mill. The cape is the most strong trait of the shore of New England, the piece opens. It stands far out, lone, into the sea, and on the map it has the air of a bar of sand.

At other parts of the shore, the mind flies at once to a snug in-land of town streets, calm farms, ponds frilled with brush, and wild blooms. At this weird thrust of land, no in-land can be called up. Wastes lie all through this reach of shore. The far town has no farm, and the soil of its plots is brought in the holds of ships.
75578-poems-of-childhood:
Poems of Childhood gathers the children's verse of Eugene Field, with illustrations by Maxfield Parrish. Scribner's Sons published the volume in New York in 1904. It joins two earlier books: With Trumpet and Drum, copyrighted in 1892, and Love Songs of Childhood, from 1894.

The contents run from Krinken and The Naughty Doll to The Sugar-Plum Tree and Little Boy Blue. Wynken, Blynken and Nod, the Dutch lullaby of three fishermen sailing in a wooden shoe, is here in full. Lullabies from many lands stand together: a Japanese lullaby, a Norse lullaby, a Jewish lullaby, and Armenian folk songs. There are fairy and nonsense pieces too, the fire-hangbird's nest, teeny-weeny folk, and Pittypat and Tippytoe. Parrish's plates gave Field's nursery classics their classic picture-book dress, and the volume has been a nursery shelf fixture ever since.
75780-william-the-good:
Richmal Crompton wrote William the Good, the ninth of her William books. George Newnes published it at London, first in 1928; this copy is the nineteenth impression of 1948. Thomas Henry drew the illustrations. The series list runs to twenty-five titles, from Just William to William and the Brains Trust. The opening tale gives the book its name. Nine chapters fill the volume.

William the Great Actor, William and the Archers, and William the Money Maker follow. William the Avenger and Parrots for Ethel come midway. One Good Turn, William's Lucky Day, and A Little Adventure close the set. The first story opens in the Christmas holidays. Ethel rehearses a play, Mrs Brown plans a whist drive, and William has influenza. He makes a very bad invalid, with none of the patience the role requires.
75886-the-mystery-of-the-kingdom-of-god:
Albert Schweitzer wrote The Mystery of the Kingdom of God, the secret of Jesus messiahship and passion, translated with an introduction by Walter Lowrie. Dodd, Mead and Company in New York issued the book in nineteen fourteen. Schweitzer had earlier written The Quest of the Historical Jesus. He gave the book to Dr H J Holtzmann, his teacher. The text in the head opens mid preface.

Behind many an assertion here lurks more detailed study of Synoptic texts than appears at first glance, Schweitzer says. For the Synoptic question the new conception of the life of Jesus is of great importance, he holds. The composition of the Synoptists appears much simpler and clearer from this point of view, he adds. The Sermon on the Mount and the commission to the Twelve were delivered much as handed down, he argues. Theology readers get Schweitzer eschatological Jesus in brief.
76602-on-old-cape-cod:
Ferdinand C Lane wrote poems of Cape Cod, with drawings by Rena V Rockwell. The second form shown here holds rights from 1961. Lane gave the book to his wife Emma. A long table lists near ninety short poems of shore and marsh.

Verse treats Monomoy, Truro hills, beach plums, dunes, and wild geese in flight. Sea shells, driftwood fires, fog, and light keepers fill the calm set. One poem hails the Cape as a region blessed of heart's desire. Readers who love the New England shore will find soft, fond lines on its winds and tides.
76666-on-the-face-of-the-flood:
On the Face of the Flood is a tale by Mary Ropes, printed at London by the Religious Tract Society. Ropes also wrote Karl Jansen's Find and Caroline Street. The contents run to twelve chapters, from The Ring That Rolled Away to Homeward Bound, with a kidnapping, a rescue, and bonds loosed along the way.

The tale opens in a Russian village of wood cutters and raftsmen, in a hut of pine trunks with cracks stuffed with tarred tow. Young Sergey, with a face as long as an axe handle, begs the foreman Matvey to hear his strange trouble and its secret. Matvey warns that the boy's uncle Abram may spy from behind the pines, and takes him home to consult his wife.
76927-only-a-clod:
Only a Clod is a novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret and Aurora Floyd, printed at London. The contents open with chapters called The Master and The Man. Ensign Harcourt Lowther, of the 51st Light Infantry, sits in his garden at Port Arthur. He watches a couple of convict gardeners go about their work with monotonous deliberation, and laments the evil fortune that stationed him there.

Tidings of home, Tredethlyn's luck, and coming home follow. Maude Hillary's adorers and the chateau de Bourbon bring in the love plot. A commercial crisis and a drama acted behind the scenes darken the middle of the book. Poor Francis, an explanation, and Harcourt gathering his first fruits come later. Rosa has her revelation near the end. The tale is a sensation novel of the school that made its unnamed author famous. It mixes colonial exile, money, and romance in due measure.
77465-the-hounds-of-god:
The Hounds of God is a romance by Rafael Sabatini, put out at Boston and New York in the late nineteen twenties. Its parts run from a lone wolf lord and a lover, through roads at Calais and a knight of the court, to flotsam, yield, and a womans prisoner. A letter, a duel of arms, and a ransom drive the mid tale.

Late parts move to a secretary of state, a queen, a friar, and the twin rocks of myth. The Holy Office looms large, with a part named in Latin word play for the hounds of the Lord. A king, his conscience, a cardinals conscience, a royal priest, and a burn rite at the stake close the arc of the plot.
77475-joe-lincoln-of-cape-cod:
McCue wrote the life of Joseph Lincoln, the famed Cape Cod tale man. His book came out in 1949 from a Cape Cod house. Richard Kelsey made the cover and the photos in it. The Boston Herald lent its files for the life work, McCue notes. Lincoln was more than a famed name, the first page holds.

His win heartens and rights men, that page goes on to say. In days when base and sour work rules, his stood clean. McCue's own list names sea, ski, and Cape books of his own. The life traces Lincoln's rise from clerk to crown of Cape tales. Home folk and fans of his books share the gain here. Warm words rule the brief.
77903-manhood:
Clement Wood wrote a plain talk book on the facts of life for men. The book is Little Blue Book number 91, from Girard, Kansas. Its rights date to 1924, and Haldeman-Julius ran the set. The Threshold of Manhood leads its list of seven parts. Youth, school aid, and growth of heart fill that first part.

The growth of love, from wild man to wed love, comes next. Mate choice, codes for men and women, and child counts stand there. Fit mates, birth curb, and the price of faults fill the mid parts. Ills from loose acts get plain talk in part six. Pure aims close Wood's blunt guide for young men.
78083-fawn-in-the-wood:
Fawn in the Wood is a fairy tale in a cheap picture edition from McLoughlin Brothers of New York. It belongs to the Yellow Dwarf series of children's chapbooks. The tale opens with a king and queen unhappy for want of a child. One day a huge crab speaks to the queen on her walk.

The crab bids her follow, promising her wish. Her longing wins over her fear, and she follows a secret path to a palace of diamonds and pearls. Six fairies stand before it, each giving her a flower made of gems. They promise her a daughter, to be called Desired, and tell her to summon them at the birth. The tale follows a classic French pattern.
78088-the-hand-of-god:
The Hand of God, by Murray Leinster, is a story of a lynch mob. A sheriff sits in a dark county jail on a hot night. Outside, a mob buzzes, bent on hanging Sam Blake for murder tonight. Blake lies in a cell, not yet come to after his capture.

The sheriff weighs the cost of a trial against election winds at home. Any jury would send Blake to the chair, he thinks with a sigh. Guns, shells, and matches are set ready on his desk in reach. Voices outside demand the prisoner awake, to know what is happening to him. Small town justice and mob heat drive the tense night scene.
78407-womanhood:
Womanhood: The Facts of Life Revealed to Women, by Gloria Goddard, is Little Blue Book number 846, published at Girard, Kansas, in 1927 and edited by Haldeman-Julius. Seven parts move from the opening door of womanhood through the origin of love, mating, the choice of a proper mate, education, the price of error, and idealism. Birth control, eugenics, courtship, and venereal disease all get plain chapters.

Goddard opens by scolding age for calling youth a golden era and gazing back with misted eyes. Such backward longing, she says, makes a race of Lot's wives, static from looking behind. Women feel it most of all. The booklet speaks frankly for its day, treating candor about love, marriage, and the body as a form of freedom for women.
78672-honest-to-doughgod:
Honest to Doughgod is a western tale by W C Tuttle, told in cowboy dialect by the hero himself. He was christened Henry Clay Peck, yet answers to Hen. His mother wanted Gilliland Van Dyke, which his father called too much name for one calf.

Hen sits on the top pole of a corral with two pals. On his left is Muley, born Lemuel Allender Bowles, a fat cowpuncher who writes poetry. On his right is Telescope Tolliver, who sings and claims Southern birth with a by gad sir. Hen plays the banjo. The three admire each other a heap, and talent runs in the group, as Hen says. One tale has Muley rustle fifteen cows and leave a poem on the gate. Range humor fans get Tuttle tall talk at full stretch.
79098-bathe-your-bearings-in-blood:
Bathe Your Bearings in Blood is a science fiction story by Clifford Simak about machines in revolt. Its headnote says every machine on earth rose, and picked Joe Crane as their test case. Crane is a newspaperman whose father's watch has served him over thirty years. One morning the watch, the wall clock, and his alarm all disagree by an hour.

The newsroom stands empty and dark an hour before the staff should arrive. Teletype machines mutter in the quiet while Crane rubs his eyes at his desk. Then something glints beside his typewriter, rat sized, shiny, and staring without eyes. He hurls a pastepot and a desk spike at the metal thing in disgust. It somersaults, rights itself on clicking feet, and dashes across the floor. The revolt of things has begun with clocks and stranger visitors.
7931-all-wool-morrison-time-today-place-:
Holman Day's All-Wool Morrison, set today in the United States across twenty-four hours, is dedicated to Percival P Baxter, champion of the people's white coal. Contents run from how the Morrison broke St Ronan's rule and the threat of night through contracts, alarms, and men waiting to be shown.

Later chapters bring a mayor's word, a thin crust over boiling lava, and a rod in pickle. A square break, flarebacks of love and mob, and rifles ruling in the people's house follow, with a capitol first in shadow, then alight. Through one tense day, Day stages politics, power, and a town's fight.
79715-the-justification-of-the-good:
Vladimir Solovyof wrote an essay on moral philosophy, rendered from Russian by Nathalie A Duddington and first published in London in 1918. Stephen Graham edited the series and added a note. Solovyof dedicated the book to his father, the historian Sergey Mihailovitch, and to his grandfather, a priest. He calls the bond between them eternal.

Graham sums up the ideas Solovyof spent his life on. They include the unity of Christendom and, beyond it, the conscious unity of mankind. Graham also names the God man, the Eternal Feminine, and love as the highest revelation. The essay sets out Solovyof's moral system at length.
832-robin-hood:
J. Walker McSpadden retold the Robin Hood legends for young readers in this clear, brisk volume. Robin becomes an outlaw, meets Little John, turns butcher to fool the Sheriff, and gathers his band in Sherwood Forest. Each chapter takes a famous exploit, from archery contests to rescues on the road.

McSpadden keeps the old ballad spirit: Robin robs the rich, aids the poor, and defies the Sheriff of Nottingham with wit and bow. The prose is plain and lively, suited to children meeting the legend first. The book remains a friendly doorway into the greenwood tales that have charmed readers for centuries.
8406-the-subterranean-brotherhood:
Julian Hawthorne opens this novel with a prisoner's footfall: a step pacing four paces in the cell above, night after night, in a sleeping jail. The narrator never sees the man or hears him speak, yet the sound becomes a bond, a brotherhood of the imprisoned. From that stark opening, the novel builds a story of confinement, guilt, and human connection behind bars.

Hawthorne, son of Nathaniel, wrote often of sin and secrecy, and here he turns to prison life itself. The book's power lies less in plot than in atmosphere: barred doors, iron walls, and the imagination filling what it cannot see. Readers of prison literature will find an early, haunting American example.
9171-slavery-ordained-of-god:
Reverend Frederick A. Ross wrote this pro-slavery book, in speeches and letters as first published, before the Civil War. His text is Romans: the powers that be are ordained of God. Ross argues in one harmonious demonstration that slavery belongs to God's government for fallen mankind, for the good of slave, master, and nation alike.

He addresses men North and South who honor the Bible and love their country, urging harmony and union on his terms. Modern readers will reject his case outright. The book remains vital evidence of how scripture was used to defend slavery, and why that defense failed.
9301-ranald-bannerman-s-boyhood:
George MacDonald wrote this boyhood tale in 1871, told by Ranald Bannerman himself. Chapters follow the glimmer of twilight, his father, Kirsty, and his first steps in life. Then comes no father, a schoolmistress defeated, and new things learned at school. Sir Worm Wymble, a kelpie, and Wandering Willie stir the boy's fancy.

Later chapters bring a fall and a dream, a bees' nest, knight-errantry, and failure, with turkey plots and old John Jamieson. A winter's ride and a peat-stack close the seasons of youth. MacDonald writes with warmth and moral clarity. The book remains a beloved Scots boy's story, tender and true.
964-the-merry-adventures-of-robin-hood:
Howard Pyle wrote these merry adventures of Robin Hood for readers who plod amid serious things. Such readers feel it shame to give themselves up, even for a few moments, to mirth in the land of Fancy. Pyle answers that life has room for innocent laughter, and he gives it in Sherwood Forest.

Robin gathers Little John, Friar Tuck, and his band, robs the rich, aids the poor, and outwits the Sheriff of Nottingham with bow and wit. Pyle's prose and pictures made this the classic Robin Hood for children. The book remains a joyful doorway into the greenwood, for readers of every age.
adventures-of-buffalo-bill-from-boyhood-: Prentiss Ingraham traces Buffalo Bill from boyhood to manhood, from early frontier scrapes to captures of outlaws and stampeding herds. The narrative piles up hunts, fights, and escapes in the dime-novel manner, presenting its hero as a scout of quick nerve and sure aim. Readers get a popular, romantic version of western life, told at speed and with broad, stirring incident.
all-wool-morrison-time-today-place-the-u: Holman Day sets All-Wool Morrison in the United States of today, with its action compressed into twenty-four hours. The Morrison breaks a school rule, assumes contracts, and answers alarms through a single crowded day, as men wait to be shown what he is made of. The novel is a brisk American tale of character tested under pressure.
annals-of-a-quiet-neighbourhood:
Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood, by George MacDonald, records a country vicar's first years among his parishioners at Marshmallows. MacDonald gives the narrator thirty four chapters of small events: despondency and consolation, a first Sunday, a first Monday, and a coffin. Visitors come from the Hall, the bishop's basin causes talk, and the new man preaches on God and Mammon to a congregation still deciding what he is.

Later chapters follow the organist, a Christmas party, and the Weir family, whose troubles fill three headings about devils in father, daughter, and vicar alike. Dr Duncan tells his story, the church rate stirs a fight, and an invalid tests everyone's patience. MacDonald writes sermons into daily life rather than the other way round: doctrine is what happens when a pastor must bury, marry, forgive, and be forgiven in one small place.
boswell-s-life-of-johnson-abridged-and-e:
James Boswell's Life of Johnson appears here abridged and edited by Charles Grosvenor Osgood, professor of English at Princeton. Osgood's preface explains his cuts: most criticism, notes, legal opinions, and letters go, while the conversation and the passages readers find by opening at random stay. Enough remains, he hopes, to illustrate the whole book.

What survives is Johnson talking: on arts propagated by Roman conquest, on biography, poetry, and men, with Boswell prompting and recording. A visitor cutting bristles from Johnson's hearth-broom as a relic shows the Doctor's fame from inside. The abridgement made the greatest English biography portable for students, and its Johnson, diverted by his own fancy, loses little of his force.
boyhood:
Leo Tolstoy continued Nikolenka's story in Boyhood, the second part of his early trilogy, in C. J. Hogarth's translation. The family leaves the estate at Petrovskoe for Moscow after the mother's death, and Nikolenka travels with his brother Woloda, their sisters, and the faithful tutor Karl Ivanitch. A thunderstorm on the road opens the boy's inner weather.

In Moscow come a grandmother's grief, bad marks at school, stolen keys, first loves, and long arguments about life. Karl Ivanitch tells his own history across three chapters. Tolstoy watches an adolescent discover vanity, cruelty, and conscience in himself, often within one page. Boyhood has less plot than Childhood and more mind: it is a diary of becoming, kept with merciless honesty.
britannica-1911-aaron-s-rod: Aaron's rod is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, and the entry gives the name two lives. In common speech it is a popular name for tall flowering plants, among them plants called hag taper and golden rod. In architecture it names an ornamental rod carved with sprouting leaves, or at times with a serpent wound round it. The figure ties to two Bible passages: Aaron's rod turned serpent in Exodus, and the rod that budded in Numbers.
britannica-1911-avenger-of-blood:
Avenger of Blood names the person, usually the nearest kinsman of a murdered man, whose duty was to kill the murderer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry places the custom in early societies, before settled government and regular criminal law grew up.

Violence was then treated as a personal injury for the victim or his kin to punish. Rules and limits kept vengeance in check in many lands. Sanctuary law offered refuge, while blood-money and the wergild let a wrongdoer buy escape from revenge. Mosaic law kept the right of vengeance but not money payment for murder. The Koran, by contrast, allows both vengeance and payment in money.
britannica-1911-black-rod:
Black Rod is the short name for the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, an officer of the House of Lords created in 1350. He is named for his staff, an ebony stick topped with a gold lion. He attends the sovereign in the upper house, keeps order there, and can arrest a peer for breach of privilege.

His best-known duty is calling the Commons to the Lords to hear a speech from the throne or royal assent to bills. The entry describes the ritual in detail. The Commons doors are shut in his face, he knocks three times with his staff, gives his name, and only then is let in to deliver the command. The custom is traced to Charles I and his attempt to arrest members.
britannica-1911-blood:
Blood, the fluid that flows in the veins and arteries of animals, is introduced in a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The first part deals not with the body but with the word itself. Blood is a word shared by many Germanic tongues. The Greek word for blood gives the prefix haemo to many compound terms.

Since life was thought to rest in the blood, the word took on many figurative senses. Phrases on cold blood, royal blood, and half blood are all parsed. Blue blood is traced to a Spanish phrase used by nobles of Castile. They claimed pure stock, shown by blue veins in fair skin. The coarse word bloody is also traced, with care, to slang use for a young rowdy lord. A science part on the body follows in the full entry.
britannica-1911-bridgebuilding-brotherho:
Bridgebuilding Brotherhood names a band of brothers, the Fratres Pontifices, who arose in the south of France in the latter part of the 12th century. Their work joined charity to building: they kept hospices at the chief fords of the great rivers, built bridges for travellers and looked after the ferries that crossed where no bridge stood.

Formal standing came in 1189, when Pope Clement III recognised the brotherhood. The notice is brief, only a few lines, but it fixes the group's place, its age, its Latin name and its three tasks of shelter, building and ferry care. For travellers in a land of wide rivers, such a body filled a real gap between charity and public works.
britannica-1911-brod:
Brod is a town of Croatia-Slavonia in the county of Pozega, on the left bank of the river Save, 124 miles by rail south-east by east of Agram. It held 7310 people in 1900. The main Bosnian railway crosses the river here to meet the Hungarian system, making the town a crossing point of real weight.

Transit trade flows through it, above all in cereals, wine, spirits, prunes and wood. To keep it apart from its twin across the river it is sometimes called Slavonisch-Brod, against Bosna-Brod or Bosnisch-Brod on the far bank. The name comes from a ford of the Save, the Servian word brod meaning just that, and the town dates at least from the 15th century. Turks and Austrians captured and recaptured it again and again, and in 1879 the Austrian army mustered here for the occupation of Bosnia.
britannica-1911-cod:
The cod is the type fish of the family Gadidae. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica spends its head on where that family sits in science. Gadids have no spines in their fins. Old schemes grouped them with herrings and pike as soft finned fish. Their closed air bladder set them apart from that group. They were then placed near the flat fishes in a suborder of their own.

Later study showed flat fishes are not their kin at all. Flat fishes turn out to be near the John Dories instead. The suborder is kept for the Gadids and two allied families. The entry then defines that suborder bone by bone. Marks include fins without spines and a tail fin of a set build. The tail is held to be a later form in the line. The fish's own habits come later in the full text.
britannica-1911-decorated-period:
Decorated Period is the name given by Richman to the second pointed, or Gothic, style of building, dated 1307 to 1377, in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Its mark is its window tracery. That tracery is geometrical at first and flowing later. The change came when the circles were dropped from window tracery. The leaves of the pattern then met and took strong reverse curves.

Flowing, or flamboyant, tracery came in during the first quarter of the century and lasted about fifty years. The arches are generally equal-sided, and the mouldings are bolder than in Early English work. The ball flower and a four-leaved flower replace the dog-tooth ornament. Capital foliage grows less stiff and more flowing, and wall patterns vary more. Chief examples named are work at Lincoln, Carlisle, York, Lichfield, and Ely. Melrose Abbey is also cited.
britannica-1911-elwood:
Elwood is a city of Madison county, Indiana, on Duck Creek, about 38 miles north-east of Indianapolis. Its population grew from 751 in 1880 to 12,950 in 1900, then fell to 11,028 in 1910. Two railways and an interurban electric line serve the city. The site was first settled under the name Quincy, and the present name was adopted in 1869. Elwood gained a city charter in 1891.

The city's fast growth as a factory centre came largely from its place in the natural gas region. When the gas supply failed in 1903, factory work fell off, though the city slowly adjusted to new conditions. It has large tin plate mills, iron and steel foundries, saw and planing mills, furniture and lamp-chimney factories, and flour mills. Brick-yards stand nearby, and the farming country round it ships grain, live-stock, and poultry through Elwood. The entry gives factory values for 1900 and 1905 to chart the boom and the slump.
britannica-1911-ephod:
Ephod is a Hebrew word of uncertain meaning, kept as it stands by the translators of the Old Testament. In the priestly writings of the 5th century B.C. and later, the ephod forms part of the high-priest's rich ceremonial dress. It was a costly object of coloured threads woven with gold, worn outside the robe. A girdle and shoulder-pieces held it in place, and from golden rings hung the breastplate, or pouch, holding the sacred lots, Urim and Thummim.

Other passages show a far wider use. The ephod belonged to the common stock of Hebrew worship, borne by Samuel at Shiloh, by the priests of Nob, and by David. Prophetic teaching came to see the ephod as against the true worship of Yahweh. The later priestly doctrine kept it, but confined it to the Aaronites alone.
britannica-1911-eros-god:
Eros, in Greek mythology, is the god of love. He is not named in Homer. In Hesiod he is one of the oldest and most beautiful of the gods, whose power neither gods nor men can resist. He also brings order and harmony out of Chaos by joining its sundered parts. In Orphic teaching this cosmic Eros sprang from the world-egg that Chronos laid in the bosom of Chaos.

That high figure sank in later mythology into the wilful god of sexual passion, son of Aphrodite and Zeus, Ares, or Hermes. He is shown as a mischievous boy, the tormentor of gods and men, from whose attacks even his mother is not safe. His brother is Anteros, god of returned love. The philosophers also made Eros the god of loyal friendship between men.
britannica-1911-fleetwood:
Fleetwood is a seaport and watering-place in the Blackpool division of Lancashire, England. It stands at the mouth of the Wyre, 230 miles north-west by north from London, at the end of a joint railway branch. Its population rose from 9,274 in 1891 to 12,082 in 1901. The town dates its rise from 1836 and takes its name from Sir Peter Hesketh Fleetwood, who laid it out. Views north over Morecambe Bay are fine, though the land behind is flat.

The two railways together form the harbour authority. The dock has gear for fast traffic, including a large grain elevator. Shipping serves the coasting and Irish trades. Steamers run to Belfast and Londonderry, with seasonal boats to the Isle of Man. Fisheries matter, salt-works stand nearby, and a promenade serves visitors. Barracks, a military hospital and a rifle range are noted. Rossall school ranks among the leading public schools of the north.
britannica-1911-food:
Food, like the verb to feed, comes from a Teutonic root, seen in Old English foda and in the word fodder. It is the general term for what is eaten by man and other creatures for the sustenance of life. The scientific side of human food is left to the articles on nutrition and dietetics. This article follows food through the stages of human life, beginning with the feeding of infants.

No food, it says, has yet been found so fit for the young of all animals as their mother's milk, though substitutes have been much sought. It quotes a French doctor who wished the state would stop mothers suckling, lest they pass on immorality and disease. From infancy the article moves through the diet of childhood, adult life and old age, weighing what a normal diet does for health at each stage of a human life.
britannica-1911-glacial-period:
Glacial Period, in the 1911 Britannica geology article, names the recent time when the whole world grew markedly colder. In northern Europe and North America, the entry says, conditions resembled those of the polar regions today. The period is also called the Great Ice Age, and it matches the Pleistocene, the earlier part of Quaternary time.

The article is long and argumentative. It notes that ice-made deposits drew serious attention only at the start of the 19th century; before that they were dismissed as rubbish, or blamed on floods. That flood view, it adds, still had defenders, and one is named. From there the article works through the evidence for land ice, the deposits it left, and the causes proposed for such a fall in temperature. It is a full survey of the ice-age question as it stood in 1911.
britannica-1911-god:
God is a word article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It treats God as the common Teutonic word for a personal object of worship. The same word serves for the gods of the old heathen myths. It also covers idols and symbols, such as an image, a tree, or a pillar.

The entry follows the word into Christian use. When the Teutonic peoples became Christian, the old word named the one Supreme Being. It named the Creator of the universe and the Persons of the Trinity. The article draws on the New English Dictionary for fine points of grammar. The old form of the word was neuter, yet Christian use made it masculine. A popular link between the word and good is also noted and set aside. Readers get a careful account of how one word grew with a people's faith.
britannica-1911-golden-rod:
Golden rod, in the study of plants, is the common name for Solidago virgaurea in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a native plant of Britain and spreads wide across the north temperate zone. Gardeners know it as an old border plant of long standing. It flowers from July to September each year. Its stem stands upright and branches with restraint. Small bright yellow heads of flowers grow in clusters along that stem.

The plant thrives in common soil with little care. Growers can spread it with ease by division in spring or in autumn.
britannica-1911-herod:
Herod is the subject of a past entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name was borne by princes of one house. That house ruled in Judaea from the year 40 before Christ. Herod the Great was the son of Antipater. Antipater backed one claimant with Arab and Roman aid. The house seems to have come from Idumaea. That root left its men open to scorn as half Jews.

Two tales of its root are set side by side. One tale, from foes, made them Philistines of Ascalon. One claim, from friends, made them Jews back from exile. The entry holds both tales as likely false. Antipater rose as the true ruler under a weak priest king. He won the trust of Pompey, Antony, and Caesar in turn. Caesar made him a Roman citizen and a governor. Herod then steps in as ruler of Galilee.
britannica-1911-hesiod:
Hesiod, the father of Greek didactic poetry, probably flourished during the 8th century B.C. His father moved from Aeolic Cyme in Asia Minor to Boeotia, and Hesiod was born at Ascra, near Mount Helicon. Feeding his father's flocks there, he took his charge from the Muses to be their poet. He dedicated to them a tripod won in a song contest at funeral games at Chalcis.

His Works and Days weaves daily life, fable and personal history into a Boeotian shepherd's calendar. One part urges honest labour against strife and idleness; a second gives rules for husbandry. A third lists lucky and unlucky days for farm and sea work. Running through it is advice to his brother Perses, who had bribed judges to strip Hesiod of his inheritance. The Theogony, on the births and order of the gods, also bears his name.
britannica-1911-heywood:
Heywood is a municipal borough in Lancashire, England, 9 m. N. of Manchester, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway. Its population was 25,458 in 1901, and it is a place of modern growth, with several handsome churches, chapels and public buildings. The Queen's Park was bought and laid out for £11,000 with money that came to Queen Victoria through her duchy of Lancaster, and opened in 1879.

Near the town stands Heywood Hall, once the home of Peter Heywood, who helped uncover the Gunpowder Plot. The town owes its rise to the Peels: the father of the first Sir Robert Peel brought its first manufactures. Heywood is a strong seat of the cotton trade, with power-loom factories, iron foundries, chemical works, boiler-works and railway wagon works. Coal is worked widely round it. The borough was incorporated in 1881 and is run by a mayor, 6 aldermen and 18 councillors, over an area of 3,660 acres.
britannica-1911-hood:
A hood is a covering for the head. The word stands in Old English as hod, kin to the Dutch hoed and the German Hut, a hat; hood and hat are distantly related. Some loose head covering, easily drawn on or off, has been natural outdoor dress at all times wherever the climate called for it. With men the hat slowly pushed it aside.

The word spreads to things shaped like a hood or doing its work: a folding carriage cover, the belled cap on a trained hawk's head, the endmost planks in a ship's bottom. In building, a hood-mould is a projecting moulding outside the arch of a door or window, weathered beneath. Stretched out level it is a dripstone.
britannica-1911-ivangorod:
Ivangorod is the subject of a brief place entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a fortified town of Russian Poland, in the government of Lublin. It lay by rail south east from Warsaw, where the Wieprz river meets the Vistula. Nine forts guarded it on one bank and three on the other.

With Warsaw and two other strongholds it formed what was called the Polish quadrilateral. That set of fortresses was meant to hold the region for Russia. The entry is short, but it fixes the town's place in a chain of defences. Readers get its rail link, its rivers, and its military role in a few lines.
britannica-1911-jarrah-wood:
Jarrah Wood, in the 1911 Britannica, is a timber entry on the wood of a great eucalyptus of south-west Australia. The tree is said to cover 14,000 square miles there. Its stems grow straight and yield squared timber up to 40 feet long. The wood is hard, heavy, and close grained, with a deep red colour like mahogany. At times its figure suits it for cabinet work.

High hopes for the wood in shipbuilding were not met in full. Its great merit is that it resists sea borers better than any other timber, and white ants as well. Well seasoned, it stands air, earth, and sea for long years, so it is prized for railway sleepers, poles, and piles. Its flaws are resin blisters and a short break under strain.
britannica-1911-jupiter-god:
Jupiter was the chief god of the Roman state. Greek influence reshaped him on the model of Zeus, the high god of the Greeks. Latin writers treated the two as one and gave Jupiter Greek myths that never belonged to Roman worship. The Jupiter of the poets is thus more than half Greek, while the Jupiter of cult stayed Roman.

At root both gods grow from one old idea: the god of light and of the sky. The earliest form of his name was Diovis pater, or Diespiter, and his special priest was the flamen dialis. The words point to a root meaning shining, kin to dies, the day. One of his oldest titles is Lucetius, the light bringer. All days of the full moon were sacred to him, and all that comes from the sky was held to be his work.
britannica-1911-murray-cod:
Murray cod, one of the largest fresh-water fishes of Australia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In spite of its name it is kin to the perch, not to the true cod. It is famed for its fine flavor as food. Its body has the perch shape, and its back fin holds eleven spines.

The spines grow shorter as the fish ages, so old fish show a lower fin. The head bones lack the saw edge found in its near kin. Its color is most often brown with a green tinge and dark green spots. The fish makes its home in the Murray River and its side streams. It is the chief food fish of those waters. It is said to pass three feet in length and a great weight.
britannica-1911-neptune-god: Neptune, an Italian god later matched with the Greek Poseidon, is the subject of a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was paired with Salacia, perhaps a goddess of salt water. In 399 before Christ he was identified with Poseidon. His feast, the Neptunalia, fell on the twenty-third of July. His temple near the Circus Flaminius held a famed sea group by Scopas. Sextus Pompeius called himself a son of Neptune. Agrippa built him a temple after the sea victory of Actium.
britannica-1911-nerchinskiy-zavod:
Nerchinskiy Zavod, a town and silver mine of East Siberia, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the government of Transbaikalia, on a small branch stream of the Argun. Its people numbered 3,000 in 1897. The entry warns not to confuse it with another town of near the same name, 150 miles away.

The town lies in a narrow valley between barren mountains, and is much better built than the other towns of its district. It has a laboratory for mine work and a weather station where readings have been taken every hour since 1842. The climate is harsh, with a mean yearly temperature below freezing and great swings of heat and cold. The wider mining district covers near thirty thousand square miles of silver mines and gold fields, cut by deep wooded valleys.
britannica-1911-philip-the-good:
Philip the Good (1396-1467) was duke of Burgundy, and this 1911 Britannica entry opens with his turn toward England. He was born at Dijon, the son of John the Fearless and Margaret of Bavaria. He followed his father in September 1419, after John's assassination.

In 1419 Philip signed the treaty of Arras with Henry the Fifth of England, owning him as regent and future heir of France. In 1420 he adhered to the treaty of Troyes, and late that year he entered Paris with the English king. In 1423 a treaty at Amiens bound him with the dukes of Brittany and Bedford, and marriages tied the houses together. A few years later cracks showed among the allies, as the entry goes on to tell.
britannica-1911-ringwood:
Ringwood, a market town in Hampshire in England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the New Forest district, south-west of London. In 1901 it held a little over four thousand six hundred people. The river Avon runs past the town in many small branches through flat meadow land.

The chief buildings named are the church of Saints Peter and Paul, the town hall, and the corn exchange. The church was rebuilt in large part in 1854. Trade in farm goods is large in the town. Local hands make farm tools, linen goods, and woollen gloves. The entry is brief, but it gives a firm fix on the town's place, size, and work.
britannica-1911-rood:
Rood, a word for a rod or pole, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. As a land measure, a rood was forty square rods, and four roods made one acre. In old English the word also meant a cross, most of all the cross on which Christ died.

That second sense shapes most of the piece. A cross figure, often with Saint John and Mary, stood above the church screen. The screen split the chancel from the nave. The cross sat on a beam or in a loft reached by a small stair. The text notes such stairs still stand in many English churches.
britannica-1911-sabicu-wood: Sabicu wood comes from a large tree of the bean family that grows in Cuba, and this very short 1911 Britannica entry praises the timber. The wood has a rich mahogany colour. It is exceedingly heavy, hard, and durable, and so most valuable for shipbuilding. On account of that durability it was chosen for the stairs of the Great Exhibition in London in 1851. In spite of the enormous traffic that passed over those stairs, the entry reports, the wood at the end was found little affected by wear.
britannica-1911-sandalwood:
Sandalwood is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a fragrant wood. The wood comes from trees of the family Santalaceae. The chief source is Santalum album, a native of India. The word runs through French, Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit forms. One old English form, sanders, is a worn down version. Use of the wood goes back at least to the fifth century before Christ. It is still much used in India and China.

Where Buddhism holds sway, the wood serves in rites. It is burned at funerals and in other ceremonies. India was the sole source until the mid 1700s. Then wood of the same kind was found in Pacific isles. That trade led to strife with the island folk. Bloodshed was common, and white traders fell victim. The text names missionary John Williams among the slain. Loss of life in that trade once topped even whaling.
britannica-1911-sapan-wood: Sapan wood, from the Malay sapang, is a red dyewood that dissolves in water. It comes from a tree of the legume genus Caesalpinia. That tree is a native of warm Asia and of the Indian islands. The wood is a bit lighter in hue than Brazil wood and its kin. Yet the same colour agent, brazilin, seems to be shared by all of them, as the brief article states in its account of the dye.
britannica-1911-saturn-god:
Saturn was a god of ancient Italy, and the Romans matched him with the Greek god Cronus, and a myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells the tale behind that match. Cronus was the youngest of the Titans, the children of Sky and Earth. Sky and Earth had other children too, the Cyclopes and the Hundred Handers. When those broods proved troublesome, Sky thrust them back into Earth.

That act vexed Earth, and she called on her sons for revenge. All of them shrank from the deed save Cronus alone. He lay in wait for his father and wounded him with a sickle. From the drops of blood that fell to earth sprang the Furies and the Giants. Cronus then reigned in the room of Sky, with Rhea as his wife.
britannica-1911-shannon-charles-hazelwoo:
Charles Hazelwood Shannon (1865- ) was an English artist, and this 1911 Britannica entry covers his style and his best-known works. He was born at Sleaford in Lincolnshire, the son of a clergyman. He attended the Lambeth school of art and was shaped by his friend Charles Ricketts and by the example of the great Venetians. His early work leaned to a heavy, low tone.

Later he gave that up for clearer, more transparent colour. He won great success with his portraits and his figure pieces in the manner of Giorgione, marked by a classic sense of style. His etchings and lithographic designs are praised too. The entry names pictures held in Dublin, Munich, Bremen, and Melbourne, and complete sets of his prints kept by the British Museum and by print rooms in Berlin and Dresden.
britannica-1911-smith-thomas-southwood:
Thomas Southwood Smith was an English doctor and reformer of public health, born in Somerset. While a student of medicine at Edinburgh he took charge of a small church flock of a free faith. He took his degree, then practiced in a Somerset town while he served a chapel there, before he moved to London.

The 1911 Britannica entry peaks with his post at a London fever sick house. His book on fever was at once taken as the standard work on the theme. In it he proved the straight link between the want of the poor and the spread of fever. The state called on him in plague years and on points of health law. His reports on ship checks, cholera, and the gains of clean towns held weight across the world.
britannica-1911-sothic-period: The Sothic period is a span of time in the old Egyptian calendar. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it by the rising of the star Sirius, called Sothis. Egypt's year held 365 days flat. The true year, fixed by that star's dawn rising, runs a quarter day longer. So the short year slipped through all the seasons over time. A full round of that slip took 1,461 years. The entry is brief and points to the main Egypt article for the full count of years.
britannica-1911-southall-norwood:
Southall Norwood is the subject of a district article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Southall Norwood is an urban district in Middlesex in England. It is a suburb of London, west of Saint Paul's Cathedral. The Great Western railway serves it, and a canal passes through it. By 1901 its people numbered over thirteen thousand, up from near eight thousand ten years before.

The article notes brick fields, flour mills, and chemical works in the district. Much of the district is made up of homes. Cattle markets are held each week under a grant from King William the Third. An old manor house from the time of Queen Elizabeth still stands. The parish church of Norwood keeps old parts in two early styles despite much repair. It holds a canopied tomb from 1547 and brass plates from the sixteen hundreds.
britannica-1911-stink-wood:
Stink-wood is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a South African tree. In botany it is known as Ocotea bullata. It belongs to the laurel family, Laurineae, in the text. Other names for it are Cape Walnut and Stinkhout. Cape Laurel and Laurel wood are also used. It takes its main name from its smell when fresh felled. That smell is strong and unpleasant to the nose.

The wood is used for building work in South Africa. A writer quoted calls it the most beautiful dark wood he has met. It is said to serve as a substitute for teak. It is held to be equally durable in use. The wood runs dark walnut to reddish brown and black. Its sap wood is yellow by contrast. The grain is extremely fine, close, dense, and smooth. Those traits make it prized for fine work.
britannica-1911-synod:
Synod is a church term explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a meeting of church officials, called by law, to debate and settle points of faith, rule, and conduct. The word is near in sense to council. In time council came to be kept for world-wide meetings, while synod served for meetings of one branch of the Church, east or west.

Provincial synods were held as far back as the second century. The article lists kinds of meeting by rank, from councils of a whole land down to the synod of a diocese under its bishop. The chief body of the Russian church bears the name of the Holy Synod. In Presbyterian churches a synod stands between the presbyteries and the general assembly. Methodist churches use the word for the meeting of a district.
britannica-1911-walmisley-thomas-attwood: Thomas Attwood Walmisley, an English musician who lived from 1814 to 1856, gets a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in London, the son of a famed organist and writer of church music. The composer Thomas Attwood was his godfather, and both men taught the boy. In 1833 he became organist of Trinity College at Cambridge. His anthems made his name there. In 1836 he was made professor of music.
cap-n-abe-storekeeper-a-story-of-cape-co:
James A. Cooper wrote a Cape Cod novel, dated 1917. Thirty-two chapters line the frame. A choice opens the tale, with Aunt Euphemia's voice first heard in talk of who shall take a girl in. Cap'n Abe and his living room come next. Shade of things to come fills the fourth place.

Night doings, a pirate boarding in jest or fright, and life under Fike fill the early run. Salt water taffy gets its own kind chapter. Doubt hangs, Louise thinks her thoughts, and a lead man steps in. Aunt Euphemia lands in force at the twelfth. Washy Gallup's prying and a pick of chaperons fill the heart. Scar, tide lift, and a soul's anchor close the heads. Store talk and shore folk form the stock.
captain-blood:
Rafael Sabatini wrote a pirate novel, in a text dated 1922, that styles its hero's tale an odyssey. Thirty-two chapters line the frame in view. A messenger opens the tale. Kirke's dragoons come next, then the lord chief judge. Human goods — men sold as slaves — fill the fourth place.

Arabella Bishop gives the love thread its name in the fifth. Plans of flight, pirates, and Spaniards fill the first sea run. The rebel convict, Don Diego, and son's duty turn the heart. Don Pedro Sangre — Blood in Spanish dress — names the hero's sea self. Tortuga, ransom, trap, and dupes mark the mid-run. The Milagrosa, thief and pirate, and the king's service fill the late heads in view. Sword, sail, and spite at wrong form the stock.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-blackwoo:
Adam Blackwood was an author born at Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1539, who died in 1613. A great-nephew of Orkney's Bishop Robert Reid, he was educated at Paris after both parents died. The bishop provided for his schooling, and Queen Mary's generosity let him finish his studies at Paris and Toulouse. At Paris he taught philosophy and published a funeral poem on Charles IX in 1574.

He also published a work on religion and government in 1575; Archbishop James Beaton then recommended him to Mary for the judgeship of the Parliament of Poitiers, where he married Catherine Courtinier. Blackwood built a good library and wrote several books, including an Apology for Kings denouncing Buchanan's views and a vigorous defence of Queen Mary, published at Paris after her death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adulteration-:
Adulteration of food, from Latin adulterare, to pollute, is defined as adding any non-condimental substance to a food, where that substance forms no portion of the food. Even this careful definition is imperfect, since heavily salted provisions may need soaking to remove salt, yet that is not adulteration. Food adulteration has long been practised, mentioned for bread by Pliny, who also notes Rome's trouble procuring pure wines.

Athens kept a public inspector of wines, and England and France early passed laws against bread adulteration. As far back as Edward the Confessor, public punishment awaited brewers of bad ale; adulteration's legal status rests largely on statute and varies by government. Food counts as adulterated if a substance depreciates or harms it. It also counts if cheaper matter is substituted, if a valuable constituent is removed, if it is an imitation, or if colouring improves its looks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-of-th:
A Spanish Carmelite called A. de Olivera, Anthony of the Mother of God was born at Leon in Old-Castile and died in 1641. At the University of Alcalá de Henares, Complutum, he taught Aristotle's dialectics and natural philosophy. Together with colleagues, he set out to make an encyclopaedia for students in arts and philosophy.

That work, first styled Collegium Complutense philosophicum and printed at Alcalá in 1624, saw further editions at Frankfurt in 1629 and at Lyons in 1637, 1651, and 1668. Thomists held it in high esteem. At first it was a treatise on logic. Over time, metaphysics and moral philosophy joined it, and it served as an introduction to the Salmanticenses' great Course of Theology. Anthony is also credited with the first three volumes of that Course.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
Confraternities devoted to the Precious Blood, the blood of Christ, first appeared in Spain. The life of Francis of the Infant Jesus, a Carmelite lay brother who died in 1601, mentions such a confraternity at Valencia. A few years on they must have been numerous, since Anna of St. Augustine, who died in 1624, welcomed collectors of alms for Precious Blood confraternities erected in many places. Ravenna in Italy had one very early, and Rome had one under Gregory XIII, later merged with the Gonfalone.

The archconfraternity as it now stands owes its origin to Mgr. Albertini, then serving at San Nicola in Carcere, Rome, where devotions to the Precious Blood had been held since 1708. Moved by the temporal and spiritual misery of the French Revolution, he joined on 8 December 1808 all willing to meditate frequently on the Precious Blood into a society. That society grew into an archconfraternity able to affiliate others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-association-o:
The Association of the Holy Childhood is a children's association for foreign missions, founded twenty years after the Society for the Propagation of the Faith, in 1843. It was founded by Charles de Forbin-Janson, bishop of Nancy in France, as the Society of the Holy Childhood. Its end is twofold. First, to gather little Christian children around the Infant Jesus from tender years. Growing in age and strength and imitating Jesus their master, they practise charity toward their own perfection.

Second, by charity and enduring liberality, those same children may help save from death and sin the many thousand children in pagan countries such as China. Those children are neglected by parents and cast away to die without baptism. The association seeks baptism for abandoned ones and, should they live, training as craftsmen, teachers, doctors, or other members of Christian communities. The entry presents child charity organized for child rescue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-she:
Blessed Thomas Sherwood, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in London in 1551, he died at Tyburn on 7 February 1578. His parents also suffered for conscience, both enduring prison for the faith. After school in 1566 he helped his father, a woollen draper, for ten years, then set out for Douai to study for the priesthood.

Spotted in Chancery Lane, he was betrayed by George Marten and examined on the pope's bull and twice racked to learn where he had heard Mass. Cast naked into a dark, foul dungeon on bare earth, with only straw from a friend's pleading, he kept a cheerful courage. Tried on 3 February for denying the queen's supremacy, he was executed four days later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-hosp:
The Brothers Hospitallers of Saint John of God carry on their founder's hospital charity from Granada across the world. John, born at Montemor Novo in 1495, turned to God's service at forty, founded his first hospital at Granada, and served the sick with heroic charity until his death in 1550. Canonized in 1690, he became patron of the dying and of all hospitals in 1898.

Antoni Martin succeeded him, Philip II funded hospitals at Madrid, Cordova, and beyond, and Pius V approved the order under Augustine's rule in 1572. Gregory XIII gave them Rome's Hospital of Saint John Calybita in 1584 as mother-house, and Marie de' Medici founded their first French hospital at Paris in 1601.
