The Revolution expelled them from forty hospitals holding 4,125 patients, yet the order now counts eleven provinces, 102 hospitals, and 12,978 beds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc:
Charles-Francois Gounod, born at Paris in 1818 and dead there in 1893, stands among the great French composers of the nineteenth century. His father died while Charles was still a child, leaving his education to his mother. At the Lycée Saint-Louis he ranked among the best scholars. His musical gifts were carefully developed by his mother.

At thirteen his mother took him to Rossini's Otello, and that same year Mozart's Don Juan raised him to high enthusiasm. Mozart remained his ideal throughout his career, and Beethoven's Pastoral and Ninth Symphonies also left lasting marks. After study at the Conservatoire under Reicha and Lesueur, he returned to Paris in 1842. His career then turned to the operatic stage, where his lyrical, sentimental treatment of Faust, Romeo and Juliet, and Polyeucte became the widest expression of French Romanticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-h:
An entry on Christopher Holywood, Jesuit, born at Artane near Dublin in 1559. His family took its name from Holywood village. Holywood studied at Padua, then joined the Society of Jesus in 1579 at Dôle, to teach Scripture and theology at Pont-à-Mousson, Ferrara, and Padua, where he knew Bellarmine. Sent to Ireland in 1598, he was seized on the way and held in the Gatehouse, the Tower, and Wisbech Castle.

Freed after Elizabeth's death, Holywood reached Ireland on Saint Patrick's Eve 1604 and published two Latin controversial works at Antwerp that year. As superior of his brethren, in an Ireland without bishops, he reconciled the lapsed, settled quarrels, and healed wounds left by persecution. Only four Jesuits stood in Ireland when he landed, but forty-two worked there at his death in 1626, with sixty more in training or teaching abroad. His letters light up the country's history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Ulrich Müller's entry follows the Most Precious Blood congregation, secular priests in community whose principal aim is missions and retreats. Members take no vows, held by charity's bond and a promise not to leave without permission. Pius VII, returning from exile, distressed at Rome's state, desired missions throughout the Papal States. He chose Gaspare del Bufalo with zealous priests in 1814, assigning San Felice convent at Giano, founded 15 August 1815.

New houses opened, and in 1820 six missions rose in the Campagna for banditti. Leo XII's 1823 election checked growth, misinformation clouding the society's standing. America received it in 1844 at Cincinnati Bishop Purcell's request, with year-long probation before brothers take fidelity promises or students begin study. Statistics count Italy's three provinces and fifteen houses, Rome, Albano, San Paolo leading, plus Spain's one province. A separate Mantua knight-order of 1608, founded by Duke Vincenzo Gonzaga with Paul V's approval, closes it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregations:
The entry surveys Precious Blood congregations, opening with the Bernadines, nuns no longer in existence, founded by Mother Ballou with Saint Francis de Sales from reformed Cistercianesses. Spiehermans founded the Daughters at Sittard, Holland, in 1862, approved by Leo XIII's decree of 12 July 1890. Girls' education and sick care form their main object. A red girdle and a cross marked F.P.S. on red ribbon distinguish them. Cardinal Mazzella served as protector, Koningbosch holds the mother-house, and they assist Holy Ghost Fathers in German East Africa, with no American foundation yet.

Sister Adorers, established on 14 September 1861, lead a further section. Sisters of the Precious Blood at Gurtweil in Baden and Grisons, Switzerland, date to 1833 under Maria Anna Brunner with her son. Statistics for 1911 count 592 professed sisters, 48 novices, 26 postulants, and 6,954 pupils across Cleveland, Fort Wayne, Kansas City, Nashville, Saint Joseph, and Tucson dioceses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-of-th:
Dominic of the Mother of God, born Domenico Barberi near Viterbo in 1792, was a Passionist theologian. His peasant parents died while he was small, and his uncle adopted him, youngest of six children. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he herded sheep and worked the farm, learning letters from a kind Capuchin and a country lad of his age. He had no regular schooling until he joined the Passionists.

Deeply religious from childhood, he felt called to the institute and to England, where he labored for the conversion of the country. He died near Reading in 1849. His letters on the English mission were printed as a supplement to the Oratorian life of Saint Paul of the Cross. The entry points readers to lives of this apostle of England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ephod:
The ephod was a garment named in Scripture, differing with its use by the high priest, by others at worship, or in idolatrous cult. For the high priest, joining Bible evidence with Josephus and Egyptian monuments, the entry distinguishes three parts: a waistcoat or bodice, two shoulder pieces, and a girdle. The bodice was a cloth bound round the body to the waist.

Its stuff was fine-twisted linen, embroidered with violet, purple, and scarlet twice-dyed threads, woven through with gold. The ephod must not be mixed up with the tunic of the ephod, a violet frock worn beneath it. Its skirt was edged with pomegranates and bells that sounded as the priest ministered. Nor is it the breastplate, a span square, set with four rows of stones naming the twelve tribes. It held the Urim and Thummim, by which the priest sought the Lord's counsel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etymology-of-:
God can be defined as the proper name of the one Supreme and Infinite Personal Being, Creator and Ruler of the universe, to whom man owes worship. It is also the common name of beings in polytheistic religions to whom Divine attributes and worship are ascribed. It is also the name applied to an idol as the image or dwelling-place of a god.

The root-meaning, from Gothic gheu and Sanskrit hub or emu, to invoke or sacrifice to, is either the one invoked or the one sacrificed to. From roots div, to shine, and thes, to implore, come deva, dyaus, deus, theos, and dia, all generic names. Also from such roots come Zeus, Jupiter, Tiu or Tiw, surviving in Tuesday, Janus, Diana, and pagan deities' names. The common Semitic name, el in Hebrew, ilu in Babylonian, and ilah in Arabic, probably means the strong or mighty one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-existence-of-:
Existence of God is a long article in two great parts: God as known by natural reason, and God as known by faith. It first states the problem against formal atheism, which it calls self-refuting, and against virtual atheism. That covers Spencer's agnosticism, which admits an Absolute but calls it unknowable, and pantheism in materialist, idealist, and mixed forms.

Among theists it weighs whether God is proved by plain inference from effect to cause, or by intuition and moral feeling. Kant denied the classic proofs to pure reason but postulated God for practical reason, a move the article says hurt theism. It then sets out proofs from causality, design, conscience, and universal consent, plus the ontological proof. The second part turns to Scripture, church councils, and whether God can be known at all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Most Precious Blood feast honours the Blood of Christ on July's first Sunday. At first only the Fathers of the Precious Blood kept its Office alone. Later it joined the Fridays of Lent in many dioceses and parishes. Baltimore's fourth provincial council adopted it in 1840.

Pius IX, exiled at Gaeta in 1849, heard Don Giovanni Merlini's plea for the feast. Rather than vow, the pope extended it at once to all Christendom. The decree of 10 August 1849 fixed it to July's first Sunday. That Sunday had fallen on 30 June, the day French troops retook Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friends-of-go:
The Friends of God were circles of devout men and women in the fourteenth-century Rhineland who sought holiness together. Born at Basle between 1339 and 1343, the movement spread down the Rhine to Strasburg, Cologne, and the Netherlands. Priests and layfolk alike joined, bound by nothing but a shared hunger for the inner life and the conversion of sinners.

From these circles rose the great school of German mystics, led by the preacher John Tauler and the writer Henry Suso. Their sermons, letters, and treatises count among the finest German prose of the age, rooted in the teaching of Saint Thomas. But a lay member, Rulman Merswin, later spread doubtful tales of a hidden master, and the whole group fell into disrepute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspard-mermi:
Gaspard Mermillod, bishop of Lausanne and cardinal, fought Geneva's Radical government for the Church's freedom. Born at Carouge in 1824, he was schooled by Jesuits at Fribourg. He became a Geneva curate in 1847, founded two Catholic journals, and built Notre-Dame, still Geneva's chief church, between 1851 and 1859 with gifts from all Christendom.

Made auxiliary bishop in 1864, Mermillod served Geneva freely for seven years and founded Oblate sisters for poor working girls. When Rome made him independent administrator, the canton banned his acts, deposed him even as parish priest, and finally expelled him to Ferney in France. He returned only after his rival's death, and full relations resumed when he became cardinal in 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-god:
God is a doctrinal article on the name, existence, nature, and relation to the universe of God, with the Blessed Trinity as its crown. It opens with the root-meaning of the word, derived from Gothic and Sanskrit roots. A Catholic Encyclopedia article argues that dogmatic atheism refutes itself and has never won reasoned assent from any considerable number of men.

By deductive analysis it treats the infinity, unity, and simplicity of God, with remarks on divine personality. It holds the world essentially dependent on God as Creator of its whole substance. It holds its continuance at every moment due to his sustaining power. The Trinity is presented as the central doctrine of Christianity: in the unity of the Godhead, three truly distinct Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-good:
Good is one of those primary ideas which cannot be strictly defined, used first as an adjective and second as a substantive. French marks the distinction with bon and le bien, and English keeps it by prefixing an article to the substantive use. A Catholic Encyclopedia article begins from everyday uses and presses toward the metaphysical question of the good.

We call a tool good if it serves its purpose, an efficient means to a desired result. We call a thing good if it fully possesses the perfections proper to its nature. A result desired for itself is a good, an end of action. The chain of means and ends must end in objects desired for themselves. Finally we speak of good conduct, a good man, and a good intention, where the adjective carries a moral sense no utilitarian reduction captures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hakon-the-goo:
Norway's King Hakon the Good, youngest son of Harold Fairhair, ruled from about 935 to 960 after a childhood at the court of Athelstan of England. They gave him his nickname Adelstenfostre and a fine education. When his harsh half-brother Eric Bloodaxe fled before discontented nobles, Hakon won the throne by promising the jarls their old rights and the freemen clemency.

Reforms in justice, government, the army, trade, and deep-sea fishing followed, with Jämtland and Värmland annexed. His Christian mission faltered: raised a Christian, he pressed the new faith until pagan strength forced him to tolerate sacrifices and even join them. Wounded by an arrow at Fitje while repelling Eric's sons, he died commending his enemy Harold as successor and was buried as a warrior in a mound.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herod:
Herod was the name of a family of rulers who loom large in the New Testament and in Jewish history, and this entry surveys them one by one. Herod the Great, son of the Idumaean Antipater, won the crown of Judea from the Roman senate in 40 BC through the favour of Octavian and Antony. He held power by shifting with Rome's changing masters, built on a grand scale, and ordered cruelties that darkened his final years.

Later Herods include Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, who had John the Baptist killed after the prophet rebuked his marriage to Herodias. Agrippa I persecuted the early church, and Agrippa II heard St. Paul's defence. The entry draws on Josephus throughout, weighs conflicting accounts, and shows how one family's fortunes tracked the rise of Roman power in Judea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-synod:
The Holy Synod, in full the Most Holy Directing Synod, is the council governing the Church of Russia and, by its example, many other Orthodox churches. Summoning a synod to settle grave questions goes back to the apostles meeting at Jerusalem over Gentile converts. Bishops, metropolitans, and patriarchs all called synods as need arose, and general councils represented the whole Catholic world from 325 onward.

Yet those synods met only briefly, for one or a few burning questions. The predecessors of modern Holy Synods lie rather in permanent councils at the courts of chief bishops, which formed naturally without harming the bishop's monarchical rule. The entry traces how that permanent council model grew into the governing synod of the Russian church and its Orthodox imitators.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hood:
A hood means a soft, cone-shaped, brimless covering for the whole head apart from the face. It may stand alone as a garment or form part of a cloak. Worn on its own, it commonly flares below into a cape of sorts, open at the front at times and at other times shut save for the face hole. Romans called it cucullus, a Celtic word, worn above all by drivers, herdsmen, and labourers.

All classes wore it as part of Roman cloaks. In the Middle Ages it was common in France, Germany, and England among clerics and layfolk, men and women, high and low. Monks and mendicant friars wore it daily, as part of their religious dress. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries it often ended in a long peak, the liripipe. Hats later displaced it, but old orders kept it, and Capuchins take their name from their hood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jasper-and-jo:
Jasper Heywood, poet and translator, was born in London in 1535 and died at Naples in 1598. As a boy he served as page of honor to Princess Elizabeth, later queen. Sent to Oxford in 1547, he took a bachelor's degree in 1553 and a master's in 1558. In 1554 he was chosen probationary fellow of Merton College, where he shone in disputations, in verse renderings of Seneca's dramas, and as Lord of Misrule at Christmas.

Anthony à Wood reports that he and his brother were wild for a spell. Jasper gave up his fellowship to head off expulsion in 1558, and later that year was chosen fellow of All Souls. Soon he gave that up over refusal to comply with Elizabeth's new religious order. He stands paired here with his father John, dramatist to his poet-translator, across Elizabethan religious change. After ordination as a priest, he was received into the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1562.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kingdom-of-go:
The Kingdom of God, called the Kingdom of Heaven in Matthew, sums up the Old Testament's deepest teaching. Kingdom here means rule or sway as much as territory: God himself reigns, and earthly kings rule only under him.

The idea runs from the theocracy sketched in Exodus, through Samuel's warning that Israel rejected God as king, and Nathan's promise to David's line. In the Psalms, God's throne stands in heaven. Prophets stress the same kingship, and Daniel's vision of one like a son of man receiving rule over all evil powers shaped what Christ's hearers expected. A rival hope, a temporal Messiah crushing nations, grew beside it, while the Book of Wisdom shows the rule lived as a just life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mazenod:
Charles Joseph Eugene de Mazenod, Bishop of Marseilles and founder of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, was born at Aix in Provence in 1782 and died at Marseilles in 1861. Sprung from a noble southern family, he showed early piety and a high, independent spirit. The Revolution drove him into exile in Italy for some years. He then studied for the priesthood, though he was his family's last representative.

Ordained at Amiens in 1811, he grieved at religion's ruin among the masses after the Revolution. In 1816 he gathered a small band to preach in the local tongue and teach the rural folk of Provence. Leo XII approved the band in 1826 as the Congregation of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate. After aiding his aged uncle, the Bishop of Marseilles, Mazenod was consecrated titular bishop in 1832 and later held the Marseilles see himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nature-and-at:
The Nature and Attributes of God treats first what natural reason knows: infinity, unity, simplicity and divine personality. Then it treats what faith adds: eternity, immensity and omnipresence, immutability, divine knowledge, divine will, and intellect and will in providence, predestination and reprobation. Reason begins from a self-existent personal First Cause distinct from matter and mind.

To say God is infinite means he is unlimited in every perfection, with every perfection his in the highest way. That differs from infinite time or space, meaning duration or extension with no fixed limit. The entry works through each attribute with careful thought, guarding against confusions, and showing how the God of the philosophers and the God of faith cohere in one Being.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nemrod:
Nemrod, also Nimrod, is the descendant of Cush, son of Ham, shown in Genesis 10 as founder of the Babylonian empire and a mighty hunter before the Lord. Hunter may be taken strictly, since Babylonian princes hunted wild beasts, or as warrior, since the original word gibbor means hero. His name has not yet been found in cuneiform inscriptions.

Attempts to identify him with known figures rest on more or less plausible conjectures. Some scholars, Delitzsch, Hommel and Haupt among them, identify him with Gilgamesh, hero of the Babylonian epic, often shown strangling a lion. Gilgamesh subdues the ox-faced Eabani, makes him his companion, triumphs over the tyrant Humbaba, and slays a monster sent by Anu and Ishtar. Like Nemrod he reigns over Erech, but the texts omit Babylon, Accad and Calneh from Genesis 10.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-servants:
The Poor Servants of the Mother of God are a religious congregation founded in 1808 by Mother Mary Magdalen Taylor with Lady Georgiana Fullerton. Taylor was the daughter of a Church of England clergyman. As one of Florence Nightingale's nurses in the Crimea she met the Catholic faith among the soldiers, and on returning to England she entered the Church.

Her friendship with Lady Georgiana led to a congregation for work among London's poor, then served by a single convent. Cardinal Manning approved and encouraged it, the Jesuits guided its spiritual training, and Leo XIII approved it in 1885. Its sisters visit the poor, teach in parochial schools, nurse the sick, and run refuges for women, with houses from London and Dublin to Rome and Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-precious-bloo:
The Precious Blood is our Divine Saviour's blood. At the Last Supper Jesus gives it the same life giving power as His flesh. Peter, John, and above all Paul treat it as one with Jesus' Passion and Death. It thus forms part of the Sacred Humanity, joined in person to the Trinity's Second Person.

In the fifteenth century divines asked whether the blood shed in the Passion stayed joined to the Word. If a core part of the Sacred Humanity, it could never part from the Word; if a mere attendant, it could. Dominicans held the first view, Franciscans the second. But since Trent called the body and blood of Jesus parts of Christ the Lord, thought has run with the Dominicans. Faber writes that the blood itself, as blood, was more than a mere attendant of the flesh.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presence-of-g:
All sound devotion must rest on truths of faith. First, faith holds that God's Essence is everywhere, in all things, through His Immensity. Faith also holds Him present in the souls of the just in a special, real, substantial way. 

To put ourselves in God's presence, or to live in God's presence, means to grow actually aware of God as present, or at least to live as if thus aware. It is a plain act, holding the print of the unseen Being with whom we hold direct dealings. His goodness to us is sure, and He loves us with an everlasting love. He keeps a special providence among us, is present everywhere, and, in Cardinal Newman's words, is heart reading, heart changing, ever open to our approach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priesthood:
Priest, from Greek presbyteros, elder, matched against neoteros, younger, means in its hieratic sense the Latin sacerdos, the Greek iereus, and the Hebrew kahane. It marks a male person called to the Deity's direct service and licensed for public worship, above all to offer sacrifice. To call the magicians, prophets, and medicine men of primitive faiths priests misuses the word. Sacrifice is priesthood's core correlative, so mere leaders of public prayer or shrine keepers have no claim to the name.

 Oldest among pagan faiths is India's, with four divisions: Vedism, Brahminism, Buddhism, and Hinduism.  St Peter calls the faithful a holy priesthood and a kingly priesthood, but the text means a figurative priesthood only. Hence the Catholic clergy alone, the entry holds, bear the name priest in truth, since they alone offer a true and real sacrifice, the Holy Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rood:
Rood, from Anglo-Saxon Rod or Rode, meaning cross, often means the True Cross itself. More broadly, the word denotes a big crucifix flanked by figures of Our Lady and St John, set above the choir entrance in medieval churches. Roods were often very large, to be seen from all parts of the church, set on a gallery, screen, or beam spanning the chancel arch.

No certain evidence dates the rood's antiquity. A silver crucifix set up by Leo III in St Peter's at Rome in 795 is sometimes claimed as an early example. Nothing proves it counted as a medieval rood. The great rood was common in almost every Western church by the thirteenth century, and certainly by the fourteenth. Figures of Mary and John were added about the fifteenth century, recalling John 19:25. Roods were usually carved wood, painted or gilded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-son-of-god:
Son of God is a title that runs through both Testaments with shifting shades of meaning. This substantial entry follows each of those meanings in turn. In the Old Testament the word son could mark any close bond. Angels, just men, and descendants of Seth could all be called sons of God. So could the whole people of Israel, and kings received the title as God's chosen rulers.

The entry then traces how the phrase deepens in the New Testament, where it belongs to Christ in a unique sense. It works through the scriptural passages and the theological questions the title raises. Readers who want to see why a familiar phrase carries so much weight will find its history laid out step by step, from Hebrew idiom to Christian doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-disibod:
Disibod, an Irish bishop who died in 700, carried his country's monastic ways into the Rhineland, and this short entry follows him there. Born about 619, he crossed to the continent around 653 and settled in the valley of the Nahe, near Bingen. Though he lived as a hermit, a community grew around him in beehive cells built in Irish fashion on the mountain slopes. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 notes his life was written in 1170 by Hildegard, from her visions.

Before his death he saw a church raised and served by monks under the Rule of Columba. He was chosen abbot-bishop, and the house took his name as Mount Disibod, later Disenberg, in the diocese of Mainz. Miracles cluster around his memory, and even his death date is disputed. Some place it on 8 September, reading 8 July as the day his relics were moved in 754, with Boniface present.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-of-go:
John of God, founder of hospital care at Granada, lived soldier, shepherd, and would-be African ransomer before he found his work. Born at Montemor-o-Novo in Portugal on 8 March 1495 to devout parents, he followed a Spanish priest to Oropeza at nine and was left with the chief shepherd there. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Granada to 8 March 1550, his fifty-fifth birthday.

To escape his master's persistent offer of his daughter's hand, John served in Charles V's army, then in a regiment bound for Austria against the Turks. Later he grieved at his birthplace for his mother's early death, shepherded at Seville, and travelled toward Gibraltar, hoping to ransom African captives with his own liberty. At Granada he built a hospital, tending patients with scrupulous care, aided by charitable priests and physicians. Heavenly guests, the entry says, sometimes lightened his herculean tasks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synod:
A synod, from Greek synodos, assembly, is a general term for church gatherings under hierarchical authority to discuss and decide faith, morals, or discipline. It matches Latin concilium, used by Tertullian a century before synodus appears in the so-called Apostolic canons, so the two words are synonyms. Bishops of the whole world under the pope form an ecumenical or general synod, the only body rightly called holy synod.

Provincial synods gather a province under its metropolitan, national or plenary synods gather a whole nation, and mixed councils join church and secular dignitaries. The diocesan synod differs from all: other councils give bishops a deciding vote, but there the bishop alone votes and legislates. Benedict XIV's De Synodo Dioecesana remains the classic work, and the entry deals mainly with diocesan synods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bridge-bu:
Bridge-building as an act of piety fills this curious entry, centred on religious associations of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Roads served pilgrims above all, and bishops granted indulgences to donors of money or labour for a bridge. Archbishop Grey of York's register supplies thirteenth-century examples of the practice.

Southern France saw regular associations formed for the work, long misread as religious orders under vows. Closer study shows guilds or confraternities instead, organised at most like a third order, wearing a habit with a badge but bound by no solemn vows. Their chapels, hospitals, and tolls reveal charity expressed in stone and timber.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-highest-g:
Philosophy's oldest question, what good should rule a life, is pursued here through Plato, Aristotle, and Thomas Aquinas. Plato calls the good the object all pursue and the reason for all action. Aristotle echoes him: the good is that at which all aim. Thomas notes the definition works backwards, from desire to goodness, yet desire remains our only way to recognise it.

Not all desires can be met, and goods clash, so some must be given up to secure others. Physical and moral goods part ways, as happiness and virtue, and their ranks prove hard to fix. Stoics, Epicureans, and Christian thinkers enter the debate, weighing pleasure, honour, and virtue against the final end of human life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-wood:
Thomas Wood, priest and confessor, was born about 1499 and died in Wisbech Castle before 1588. He held a string of posts under Mary, including a prebend at Canterbury, rectories in Essex and Middlesex, and a stall at Westminster Abbey. He was also one of Queen Mary's chaplains, and at her death he was nominated for the bishopric of St. Asaph.

Elizabeth's settlement cost him all three of his chief benefices in 1559. Arrest followed for his religion: the Marshalsea in 1560, the Fleet in 1561, the Tower in 1569, where he faced threats of the rack, and the Marshalsea again in 1571. He was still there in 1579, aged eighty, and in July 1580, a prisoner for the old faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-truce-of-god:
A temporary suspension of hostilities, distinct from the Peace of God, which is perpetual and narrower in scope. The Peace covers consecrated persons, places and times: clerics, monks, churches, monasteries, cemeteries, Sundays and feast days, with excommunication for transgressors. It was extended to the poor, pilgrims, crusaders and travelling merchants.

The Truce dates only from the eleventh century and arose amid feudal anarchy, when private wars made Europe a battlefield of castles and armed bands. A Council of Elne in 1027 forbade hostilities from Saturday night until Monday morning. That canon was the germ of a ban later stretched across further days of the week.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-lock:
John Lockwood was a priest and martyr born about 1555 who died at York on 13 April 1642. Eldest son of Christopher Lockwood of Sowerby in Yorkshire and Clare Lascelles of Sowerby and Brackenborough Castle, he reached Reims with his younger brother Francis on 4 November 1579. He was at once sent to Douai for philosophy. Francis was ordained in 1587, but John entered the English College at Rome on 4 October 1595.

Ordained priest on 26 January 1597, he was sent on the mission on 20 April 1598. After imprisonment he was banished in 1610, but he returned, was seized again and condemned to death, then reprieved. Finally captured at Wood End, Gatenby, at the home of Bridget Gatenby, he was executed with Edmund Catherick, closing a mission career of over forty years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wigbod:
Wigbod, also Wicbodus, Wigbold, or Wigbald, was an eighth-century theological writer whose surviving work is a Latin commentary on the Octateuch. Questions on the Octateuch, covering the five books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, and Ruth.

Its form is a dialogue between pupil and teacher, the pupil raising difficulties and the teacher solving them. Wigbod composed none of the answers himself, instead quoting verbatim eight Fathers: Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, Ambrose, Hilary, Isidore, Eucherius, and Junilius. For most of Genesis only Jerome and Isidore are used, later Isidore almost alone. The Maurists Martène and Durand, finding the manuscript at St Maximin's, Trier, printed only the portion through Genesis's first three chapters. The work's chief value lies in preserving its quoted Fathers' texts. Three Latin hexameter poems precede the commentary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-lyndw:
William Lyndwood was Bishop of Saint David's and the greatest English canon lawyer of his age. Born about 1375, he died in 1446. He became the Archbishop of Canterbury's official, his chief law adviser, in 1414, Dean of the Arches in 1426, and Archdeacon of Stow in 1434. On Henry VI's warm recommendation, he became Bishop of Saint David's in 1442. He also served Chichele against the Lollards and acted as clergy spokesman to the crown on subsidies.

Lyndwood travelled widely as a diplomat to Portugal, France, and the Netherlands, served as royal proctor at Basle in 1433, and negotiated political and trade treaties. His fame rests on the Provinciale, a gloss on English provincial council decrees arranged like Gregory IX's Decretals, picturing clergy opinion on every subject. Maitland used it to demolish the claim that papal canon law bound no English church court, a point later law books confirm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-sherw:
William Sherwood was Bishop of Meath whose feud with the Earl of Desmond shaped Irish politics in the 1460s. His earlier life is unknown; he died at Dublin on 3 December 1482. He gained the see by papal provision in April 1460 and clashed with Thomas Fitzgerald, eighth Earl of Desmond, deputy to the Duke of Clarence as lord-lieutenant. Desmond charged him with plotting the murder of his followers, and in 1464 both men laid their grievances before Edward IV in England.

Edward backed Desmond, cleared by the Irish parliament of disloyalty and treasonable Irish dealings. When Desmond fell in 1467 and the Earl of Worcester succeeded him, Sherwood was suspected of driving the opposition that sent Desmond to the scaffold. Years later Sherwood became deputy, but his rule proved so unpopular that he was removed in 1477 after two years. He held Ireland's chancellorship from 1475 to 1481 and lies buried at Newton Abbey near Trim.
charred-wood:
Francis Clement Kelley's novel appeared in 1917 under the name Myles Muredach, with illustrations by J. Clinton Shepherd. Its motto asks whether the Designer must char the wood before drawing with it. Mark, the hero, first lies in tall grass beside the wall of the Killimaga estate, watching the bluff road above the sea.

A lady steps from a tree, and mystery follows her. Monsignore, a bishop, and Father Murray of Sihasset draw Mark into church circles under suspicion. Who is Ruth? One chapter asks it outright. An abduction, a woman who declares she is not the duchess, and a confession build the puzzle. Saunders scores points as the truth nears. The title's meaning lands in the final chapter.
childhood:
Leo Tolstoy made his name with Childhood, a short novel told by Nikolenka Irtenev, a boy of ten on a Russian country estate. Tolstoy was a young officer when the book first appeared, and C. J. Hogarth translated this edition. Nikolenka watches his German tutor Karl Ivanitch, his gentle mother, and his older brother Woloda with painful honesty.

Scenes move from lessons and birthday presents to hunts, dances, and a death that ends the boy's safe world. Nikolenka swings between love and shame, catching his own feelings in the act. Readers meet Tolstoy's gift early here: small moments, exact feelings, and a child's view that spares nobody, least of all himself.
clara-hopgood:
Clara Hopgood, by Mark Rutherford, studies conscience in a fen country town. Rutherford was the pen name of William Hale White. T Fisher Unwin printed this third impression in 1907. The first edition appeared in March 1896. Its title page names an editor, Reuben Shapcott, his other invented self. The story opens at Fenmarket, in the Fens, ten miles from Eastthorpe.

White notes that all roads out of Fenmarket run level. They run monotonous too, unlike the hill country at Eastthorpe's edge. The flatness suits his subject. Clara and her sister Madge Hopgood grew up in a strict Nonconformist home. Dissenters outside the Church of England shaped that home. Courtship, religious doubt, and family duty now test both sisters. Everyone watches everyone else. White wrote about provincial dissenting life from inside it. Ordinary happiness, refused and accepted, does the testing.
confessions-of-boyhood:
Confessions of Boyhood, by John Albee, published by the Gorham Press of Boston, is a memoir of a New England childhood told in titled chapters. The Walls of the World opens it. The contents read like a life in stations: Holidays, The Amputation, Country Funerals. My Mother's Red Cloak, My Uncle Lyman, and The Dorr War and Millerism follow.

Apprenticeships fill the second half: the saw mill, bootmaking, shop boy, pistol maker, then an awakening, student life, school master, and farm hand. The opening chapter lingers on the early New England farmhouse, low built like a Greek temple and beautiful in its place. His own apprenticeship terms promised a new suit yearly and summer schooling; the clothes never came, his mother furnished them, and he went barefoot seven months of the year.
doe-osti-17171707-advancing-beam-diagnos:
Orator Murambiwa, Deepak Rai, and Jonathan Quemuel of Los Alamos describe a rebuilt wire mapping system for beam position and phase monitors, issued 3 August 2026. The monitors, called BPPMs, read where a charged particle beam sits inside the pipe. Los Alamos Neutron Science Center runs over a hundred of them, and each is calibrated before installation.

Calibration moves a wire carrying a 201.25 megahertz radio signal through the monitor opening, standing in for the beam, while four electrodes record signals. The old mapper's aging hardware hurt repeatability and upkeep. The modern system pairs updated radio gear and Zaber motion control with a Python interface and a PyQT control panel. Automated scanning and calibration file output come next, after validation runs finish.
doe-osti-2589607-supply-chain-improvemen:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11539R covers a laboratory project by Hannah Sims, Alexander Wilson-Heid, Brandon Langdon, and co-authors on printing parts from tantalum. Tantalum is a refractory metal: it resists heat and corrosion across a wide range of acidity, and it is used in capacitors, medical implants, and reactor parts. It is also costly, hard to melt, and reactive, which makes bulk shaping difficult.

The project aimed to strengthen the domestic supply path and replace aging legacy materials. Trials printed demonstration shapes tied to mission needs, adjusted for security, and the team fitted an oxygen and moisture scrubber from glovebox practice into the printing setup. Clean air matters because hot tantalum grabs oxygen fast. Results support printing as a workable route for small, high-value refractory parts.
doe-osti-3005746-benchmarking-a-defeatur:
Eric He and Charles Yeamans of Lawrence Livermore check a simulation against reality in report LLNL-TR-2013887, dated November 2025. The simulation is a defeatured, simplified Geant4 model of the National Ignition Facility. Simplified models run fast enough for routine analysis, but only if their answers track the real machine. Neutron measurements provide the ground truth here.

Two data sets do the checking: HTOAD and HNED neutron measurements, the latter from activation foils placed at several positions. Tables compare predicted and measured activation for gold, indium, titanium, nickel, aluminum, and zirconium foils at neutron yields near 3.9 times ten to the fifteenth. Agreement across elements and positions is what benchmarking means in practice. The report gives modelers a stated basis for trusting the fast model.
doe-osti-3014788-modular-biomass-gasific:
A University of North Dakota final report under award DE-FE0032182 covers modular biomass gasification for joint hydrogen and power production. It was submitted January 28, 2026 and revised April 30, 2026. Envergex and Singularity Energy Technologies partnered on it. The project ran from October 2022 through September 2025. Junior Nasah was principal investigator.

A central thread is the oxygen carrier material. It moves oxygen through the gasifier. The team manufactured carriers at lab scale. They characterized them and tested their working life. Thermogravimetric runs mapped iron oxide kinetics. Reduction temperatures stepped from 720 to 820 degrees Celsius in 20-degree increments. Samples weighed roughly ten milligrams. Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide each made up 22.5 percent of the reduction flow. Recommendations for future work close the report.
doe-osti-3017522-process-intensification:
Kevin J Whitty and Jieun Kim of the University of Utah wrote this final report for award DE-FE0032174, dated January 2026, with Idaho National Laboratory as partner. The project intensified hydrogen production through sorption-enhanced gasification of biomass. Gasification turns biomass into gas; adding a sorbent that grabs carbon dioxide as it forms pulls the chemistry toward more hydrogen.

Work ran from feedstock preparation to process development unit studies. Biomass was characterized, pelletized, and also pelletized premixed with limestone, the calcium source for the sorbent. Lab studies measured gasification rates and tested ways to maximize hydrogen output. One mechanism got close attention: carbon monoxide and hydrogen may compete with carbon dioxide for active sites on the calcium oxide surface, cutting absorption. The report follows that question into larger-scale runs. Hydrogen producers get a tested route from farm residue to a cleaner gas stream.
doe-osti-3028593-quantitative-evaluation:
Mariah L Garcia and Kyle A Clavier of Sandia National Laboratories put numbers on potassium iodide policy in SAND2026-19267, printed March 2026. Potassium iodide tablets, taken during a reactor accident, flood the thyroid with stable iodine so radioactive iodine is turned away. Planners must decide who gets tablets, where they are stocked, and how that interacts with evacuation. This study scores the strategies by dose avoided.

Accident scenarios drive the math. In the long-term station blackout case, the atmospheric release begins 45.3 hours after the accident starts, a delay that changes everything: cases with immediate evacuation end at zero dose. Results are given at two and five miles for total effective dose and for adult and child thyroid doses. Figures trace how the normalized doses fall with distance for each distribution scenario.
doe-osti-3363428-manufacturing-valuable-:
The Institute for Advanced Composites Manufacturing Innovation led this Southern Appalachia project (award DE-FE0032045). Charles Sims of the University of Tennessee was the principal investigator. Partners included Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the geological surveys of Alabama and Tennessee. The project ran from October 2021 to December 2024 under the CORE-CM initiative. It sought routes to rare earth elements and critical minerals from coal and coal waste. It also sought carbon based products from the same feedstocks.

The thick final report mixes resource assessment with laboratory characterization. Microscopy and spectroscopy showed rare earth bearing fluoro-oxides and monazite in coal ash. Their occurrence ties closely to how the elements sit in the raw coal. The aim throughout was new industry for distressed coal communities.
doe-osti-3366047-extension-of-clad-damag:
Argonne National Laboratory report by Aydin Karahan, dated March 31, 2026, extends a reactor safety model inside the MOOSE SubChannel Module. The Clad Damage Propagation model tracks what happens after fuel cladding fails in a sodium-cooled fast reactor. The extension follows the fission gas that escapes: where it disperses, and how the resulting two-phase coolant flow degrades heat removal from neighboring pins.

New physics includes channel-averaged void fraction from a Lockhart-Martinelli framework, two-phase pressure drop multipliers, inlet flow loss at fixed core pressures, and heat transfer penalties tied to void intensity. Radial gas plume spread is calibrated from mineral-oil jet experiments, mapped to sodium through Reynolds-Weber similarity. Demonstration runs on 19-pin and 37-pin bundles show the coupled behavior that safety analysts need.
doe-osti-3367489-user-s-manual-for-resra:
Argonne National Laboratory manual ANL/EVS-25/27 Volume 1, by C. Yu, S. Kamboj, J.-J. Cheng, D. LePoire, C. Wang, and E. Gnanapragasam, explains the methodology behind RESRAD-RDD&IND version 2, Argonne's code for radiological dispersal device and improvised nuclear device events. After a dirty bomb or nuclear detonation, officials need operational guidelines: when to evacuate, when to relocate people, and when areas can reopen. The code derives those guidelines from dose models rather than improvisation.

Volume 1 lays out the guideline groups, from access control through relocation, and the exposure scenarios behind them; one rural relocation case assumes a resident spends 16.4 hours daily indoors and 7.6 outdoors. Dose-to-source ratios connect measured contamination to first- and second-year doses, compared against federal protective action guides. The June 2026 manual serves emergency planners.
doe-osti-3367490-user-s-manual-for-resra:
Argonne National Laboratory manual ANL/EVS-25/27 Volume 2, by S. Kamboj, C. Yu, D. LePoire, and colleagues, is the user's guide companion to the RESRAD-RDD&IND methodology volume. Where Volume 1 explains the dose models, Volume 2 walks the analyst through the software itself: installing from the RESRAD website, checking the installation, starting the code, and completing its input forms.

Scenario inputs get careful treatment. Each scenario carries its own exposure begin time. An Edit Table option lets users replace yield-based radionuclide estimates with measured ground concentrations. That resets the table for hand entry and locks the exposure start to the measurement time. The June 2026 guide targets the emergency-response analysts who run the code during exercises and real events.
doe-osti-3383002-community-solar-project:
Community Solar Project Models, an introduction to basic financial and organizational models by Simon Sandler, Jenna Harmon, and Sonja Berdahl, explains the ownership and billing structures a shared solar project can take. Community solar lets subscribers buy into one installation. No roof panels are needed. The guide's premise is that the model chosen decides who pays, who is paid, and who does the work.

Utility-owned projects are financed, hosted, and operated by the utility. The utility collects subscription payments and returns a bill credit. Florida Power and Light's SolarTogether and Austin Energy are the case studies. Other chapters cover third-party ownership with consolidated or dual billing. They cover cooperative ownership on either side of the meter. Multifamily housing projects under master metering or net metering follow, along with community benefit funds. Case studies sit in an appendix.
doe-osti-3827850-ffiam-full-field-irradi:
Sandia report SAND2026-26194, printed September 2026, introduces the Full-Field Irradiance Analysis Model for the OpenCSP software set. Cianan Sims and Daniel Small are the printed authors, and Sims Industries built the model for the lab. When a solar tower field idles, its mirrors park in standby aim patterns. Parked mirrors still bounce sunlight into the sky, sometimes into bright hazard zones. FFIAM maps that light through the whole airspace, cell by cell.

Users feed in field layouts and mirror designs, or import them from data files. Two workflows follow: one crunches numbers, the other draws maps and moving views. Outputs include heat maps and flight-path exposure charts. Aim strategy drives the hazard shape. A single aim point stacks light into one fierce column above the tower. A ring pattern spreads the same light wide and thin. Site tests centre on the National Solar Thermal Test Facility.
dragon-s-blood:
Henry Milner Rideout set his 1909 adventure novel Dragon's Blood in a China of treaty ports and river gunboats, with pictures by Harold M. Brett. A warm letter at the front gives the book to Charles Townsend Copeland of Harvard, in the words of Kipling's Peachey Carnehan. The hero, Rudolph, stands at the center of a crowd of traders, soldiers, and spies.

Chapter heads run from A Lady and a Griffin through a siege, a Hakka boat, and the dragon's shadow. War boards, pagodas, and a white lotus sect fill the middle. In one talk, officers agree on a grim plan: stock one house well, and fortify it if the pinch comes. Rideout writes the China coast as a place where trade and arms sit at the same table, and young Rudolph must learn fast which men to trust.
eastman-indian-boyhood:
Charles Eastman, a Santee Sioux writer and doctor, published Indian Boyhood in 1902. Eastman, also called Ohiyesa, grew up in the traditional way before his father took him into white schooling. The memoir looks back at that first world with love.

He describes hunting lessons, games, storytelling around winter fires, and the teaching of his grandmother and uncle. His people were then living the last years of free life on the northern plains. The reservation era was closing in as he wrote. Indian Boyhood became a beloved classic, the first of his many books joining Native memory to American letters.
elsie-s-motherhood:
Martha Finley, writing also as Farquharson, carries her heroine into marriage and children in Elsie's Motherhood, dated 1876, the fifth volume of the series. Her preface owns a bold choice. Friends urged her to bring in the doings of the Ku Klux, to give a truer picture of the South in 1867 and 1868.

Finley says she worked from the published reports of the Congressional Committee of Investigation, and kept within the facts there given. The Klan's proceedings, the government's clemency, and northern kindness to the suffering South all enter the tale. At home, Mr. Travilla promises a captive guest that they will make amends for the loss of liberty, and rides to Fairview for news of family. The volume mixes nursery tenderness with Reconstruction violence, a pairing few children's series attempted.
elsie-s-womanhood:
Martha Finley brings her heroine to marriage in Elsie's Womanhood, entered in 1875 by Dodd and Mead, a sequel to Elsie's Girlhood. Her preface faces a hard fact: dates compelled her to bring in the late war. She vows to treat it so as to wound the feelings of none, impartial as if writing history.

The war's losses and sufferings on both sides, she hopes, will make any renewal of the strife abhorrent to every lover of humanity. For the Teche country she thanks Edward King's Old and New Louisiana. At home, Elsie appears before her guests in pure white, lovelier than lily or rose, as Aunt Wealthy cries. The volume crowns the girlhood books: the pious child becomes a bride on the edge of a nation's wound, and Finley pleads for one people, one language, and one God.
every-step-in-canning-the-cold-pack-meth:
Gray's Every Step in Canning teaches the cold-pack method for home food preservation. Grace Viall Gray was formerly associate professor of home economics at Iowa State College. The book is dated 1920. Its contents run from first preparation to marketing home canned goods.

Chapters cover soft fruits, hard fruits, vegetables, soups, and meats. Jellies, jams, preserves, and fruit juices get their own chapter. Tin canning and fractional sterilization are treated as special methods. Later chapters turn to drying, brining, curing, and egg preservation. The first chapter recalls how war revived home canning after years of store buying. Gray writes for housewives who must waste nothing and can with care.
faith-gartney-s-girlhood:
Whitney's Faith Gartney's Girlhood follows a young woman's path through work and duty. A. D. T. Whitney wrote the novel, here in a 1913 New York edition. Faith's aunt Henderson and her friend Glory McWhirk shape the early chapters. The contents run to thirty-seven chapters in all.

Money opens the tale as its first chapter title and theme. Aunt Henderson's Girl Hunt and A Niche in Life set Faith's search for a place. Chapters such as Life or Death and Rough Ends mark strain. A Leading, Paul, and Roger Armstrong's Story deepen the middle. At the Mills and Locked In bring crisis near the end. Aunt Henderson's Mystery resolves late, before Christmastide and a wedding journey. Whitney writes a earnest girlhood of conscience and care.
fires-of-driftwood:
Mackay gathers her poems in Fires of Driftwood, first published at Toronto in 1922. Isabel Ecclestone Mackay had placed the verses in magazines on both sides of the border. J. E. H. Macdonald made the decorations. The contents range from the title poem to Lake Louise, The Prairie School, and Calgary Station.

The sampled poems show her range. One gives a child love as a rose, and death as a greater boon still: when the rose has withered, the child may pass out, smiling, and close the gate. Another walls the speaker in a town with two gates. She loves its narrow ways and common sun. But she shuns the second gate, and feels cold fingers on her heart when she glances that way. Mackay's verse is clear, musical, and rooted in Canadian ground.
handbook-on-japanning-2nd-edition-for-ir:
William N. Brown first published his handbook on japanning and enamelling in 1901, and this second edition, revised and enlarged with thirteen illustrations, came out at London in January 1913. Japanning is the craft of giving wood, tin, and iron a hard, glossy, colored coat, in the manner of Japanese lacquer. Sections on tin-plating and galvanizing go with the main art. The publisher was the house of the Oil and Colour Trades Journal.

The contents start with priming and preparing the surface, then take up japan grounds color by color, white first and blue after. Recipes, stoving, and repair fill the practical pages. The book was written for working japanners and for amateurs with small shops. It keeps a vanished trade's know-how in plain terms: how trays, bicycle parts, and tinware got their shine.
hofmannsthal-der-tor-und-der-tod:
A shallow aesthete who has admired life instead of living it meets Death face to face in Hofmannsthal's Der Tor und der Tod, given here in German. Death and the Fool, written when the poet was nineteen, stages that reckoning in a single night. Claudio's beautiful rooms and collected treasures suddenly testify against him.

Figures from his past return to show him the loves and duties he let slip away unused. The verse play meditates on art, life, and mortality with stunning maturity. Its announcement of a genius was unmistakable to its first audiences. Short enough to read at a sitting, it leaves a long echo. The work still opens many editions of Hofmannsthal, rightly placed first.
in-the-clutch-of-the-war-god:
Milo Hastings wrote In the Clutch of the War-God as a future-war tale, run in Physical Culture magazine in 1911. Bernarr Macfadden's foreword says Hastings dipped into the future to warn a complacent America. The frame calls it a chronicle of the Orient's invasion of the Occident. Ethel Calvert is warned by her servant Goyu to be ready to flee.

Planes by the thousand form a bluff of a great invasion in one scene. Komoru tells Ethel they will not attack the town, only seem strong. Fear, flight, and war plans drive the short tale. It reflects period anxiety about Asia and American readiness.
love-songs-of-childhood:
Love-Songs of Childhood is a book of children's verses by Eugene Field. Field dated his dedication at Chicago on November 1, 1894. He lays the songs at the feet of the aunt who once rocked him to sleep. The contents list the Rock-a-By Lady, the Night Wind, and Kissing Time.

Verses here tell of gardens, cradles, storks, and the Dinkey-Bird. 'Jest 'Fore Christmas' and the Duel bring fun and mischief. Field mixes lullaby tenderness with sly humor for older readers. His 'Wynken, Blynken, and Nod' became America's best-known lullaby poem. The book made him the beloved children's poet of his age.
magnum-bonum-or-mother-carey-s-brood:
Magnum Bonum, or Mother Carey's Brood, is a family novel by Charlotte M. Yonge. The contents open with Joe Brownlow's fancy and a brood of 'chickens.' Mother Carey is a widow raising her children on small means. Her late husband left behind a secret he called his magnum bonum.

That 'great good' is an invention that might make a fortune. Chapters weigh brains against no brains, and flight against duty. An offer comes for the magnum bonum, testing the family's honor. Ellen's own magnum bonums prove to be of another kind. Yonge writes of home, sacrifice, and steady faith. It is among her warmest tales of family life.
marie-bashkirtseff-from-childhood-to-gir:
Marie Bashkirtseff: From Childhood to Girlhood draws on her famous journal. Mary J. Safford translated these pages from the French. Marie began her journal at twelve years old. She wrote, the editor says, ingenuously and sincerely, in notebooks bound in white parchment.

Her whims amuse, her enthusiasms thrill, and her sufferings touch the reader. The editor prized the book for revealing a young girl's true mind. Children, she notes, hide their real selves from grown-up people. Marie hid nothing: her irony and ambition fill every page. Very few documents show childhood from inside so clearly. These early notebooks open the soul of a remarkable girl.
my-boyhood:
John Burroughs recalls his youth on a New York farm in this memoir. His son Julian wrote the foreword and a closing part. Julian says his father wrote in self-defense against his own draft. The old farm sat high on the side of Old Clump.

Burroughs loved his birthplace and was homesick for it for years. Hills, chores, woods, and first books fill his sketches. A poem called Waiting opens the contents with calm faith. The memoir shows how a farm boy became America's famed nature writer. Its plain, fond voice makes the lost farm world live again on the page.
nasa-tm-19650014315-a-wind-tunnel-invest:
Langley researchers tested rounded nose shapes, called bodies of revolution, in a high Mach number jet at very high speeds. Angles of attack went all the way to ninety degrees, far beyond normal flight. The shapes began as a pointed nose, then were changed step by step in the tunnel program.

Blunting the nose, changing a hollow nose face to a rounded one, and adding afterbodies were all tried in turn. Results showed that planform area and its spread mattered more than the exact nose shape or sharpness. A cross-flow drag theory matched the measured normal-force data well in the comparison. Such high-angle data matter for missiles and for reentry shapes that must stay stable.
nasa-tm-19690000779-application-of-the-c:
John D. Warmbrod and Heinz G. Struck of Marshall Space Flight Center present a calculation method for tube wind tunnels in this August 1968 memorandum. The method computes one-dimensional, time-dependent compressible flow through a pressure-tube wind tunnel. Designers need such predictions before building and running a new tunnel.

The procedure uses the method of characteristics for unsteady flow of a perfect gas. It accounts for area changes, shock formation, and crossing discontinuities in the flow. A Fortran computer program for the CDC 3200 machine accompanies the method. Input preparation is described in detail. Calculated results are shown for a pressure-tube tunnel then under construction at Marshall.
nasa-tm-19720023239-nasa-dod-earth-orbit:
R. E. Kincade, M. E. Donahoo, and W. R. Pruett wrote this NASA internal note in July 1971. They worked in the Flight Analysis Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. Their subject was how a planned Earth orbit shuttle might carry payloads for NASA and the Defense Department.

The note builds traffic models based on loading payloads from end to end. It sets out spacecraft plans and space missions, and it counts flights and payload needs. It also weighs two possible reusable tugs for moving loads in orbit. Planners could use such models to judge how much traffic the shuttle system had to handle.
penrod: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Penrod, the dedication, contents, and the first sentence of chapter one, with no more story text visible. The title page names Booth Tarkington. The contents promise thirty-one chapters of a boy's scrapes, among them a boy and his dog, the pageant of the Table Round, the smallpox medicine, tar, and a birthday party. The opening line sets Penrod morosely on the back fence, envying Duke, his wistful dog.
queen-victoria-her-girlhood-and-womanhoo:
Queen Victoria: Her Girlhood and Womanhood, by Grace Greenwood, is a life of the Queen written for younger readers, opening with a letter that dedicates the book to Camilla Toulmin, Mrs. Newton Crosland, of Blackheath Park. The letter looks back to the days when the Victorian era itself was young.

In her preface Greenwood owns that the book was written in under three months. There were delays while she hunted facts about the Queen's early life. A serious trouble of her eyes delayed her too. Its style, she warns, is free and easy, formed by years of newspaper work, and new for the grave business of biography.
ranald-bannerman-s-boyhood: Ranald Bannerman's Boyhood, by George MacDonald, dated 1871, is shown here by its contents alone. The chapters run from an introductory and The Glimmer of Twilight through My Father, Kirsty, I Begin Life, and No Father, then school and trouble: Mrs. Mitchell Is Defeated, A New Schoolmistress, Sir Worm Wymble, two kelpie chapters, Wandering Willie, Elsie Duff, A New Companion, and I Go Down Hill, with the trouble still growing.
records-of-a-girlhood:
Frances Ann Kemble, the actress known as Fanny Kemble, recorded her early life in this memoir, issued in a second edition by Henry Holt of New York in 1880. Parts of it first ran in the Atlantic Monthly. A note at the front says much new matter was added and the whole was revised.

Kemble begins with a set of her own letters, written over forty years and sent back to her by a friend. The letters, in their thousands, form a history of her life as she lived it. Her girlhood in a famed stage family, and the start of her own career, lie ahead in that record.
representative-plays-by-american-dramati:
Montrose J. Moses edited this set of representative plays by American dramatists, dated 1856-1911 on its title page, and issued it in 1921. Each play carries his introduction, and portraits and original playbills picture the set. He dedicated the book to Brander Matthews, friend of the American theatre.

Ten plays fill the contents. Rip Van Winkle, in Charles Burke's version of 1850, leads, and Francesca da Rimini by George Henry Boker follows. Love in '76, Paul Kauvar, and Shenandoah carry the set through the century's turn. In Mizzoura, The Moth and the Flame, The New York Idea, The Easiest Way, and The Return of Peter Grimm close the list.
robin-hood:
J. Walker McSpadden retells the Robin Hood ballads in twenty chapters of prose, each headed with how the deed was done. The first tells how Robin Hood became an outlaw. Then come his meetings with Little John, Will Scarlett, and Friar Tuck, the three most famed of his merry men.

Robin turns butcher and enters the Sheriff's service in one chapter, and Little John enters it in the next. Allan-a-Dale's wooing is prospered, a widow's three sons are rescued, and Robin fights Guy of Gisbourne. Maid Marion comes back to Sherwood Forest, the outlaws shoot in King Harry's tourney, and the Bishop is dined and then goes outlaw-hunting. Will Stutely's rescue closes the list shown.
roman-mosaics-or-studies-in-rome-and-its:
Hugh Macmillan, D.D., gathered these studies of Rome and its neighbourhood in a book from Macmillan of London and New York in 1888. He had written Bible Teachings in Nature and Holidays in High Lands before it. Chapter one takes A Walk to Church in Rome, street by street.

The walk passes his residence in Capo le Case, the church of San Giuseppe, and the Pillar of the Immaculate Conception. The Piazza di Spagna, its staircase, models, and beggars follow, then the Via Babuino and the Piazza del Popolo. Chapter two turns to the Appian Way, its tombs, its loneliness, and its restoration, in the same close-watched manner.
rookwood:
William Harrison Ainsworth's novel Rookwood, dated 1834 in its heading, appears here from the Rittenhouse Press of Philadelphia. Thackeray's phrase, the immortal Ainsworth, heads the title pages, and the New York Herald is quoted for the book's vivid picture of its times and places. A frontispiece shows Dick Turpin clearing Hornsey toll-gate.

A table of contents supplied by the transcriber, not present in the original, maps the book. A memoir and a preface stand before Book One, The Wedding Ring. Its first parts are named The Vault and The Skeleton Hand, gothic titles for the tale that follows.
seekers-after-god:
Rev. F. W. Farrar, Canon of Westminster, wrote these lives of pagan thinkers who reached toward truths that Christians hold. The Seneca section opens the book. Farrar begins in Cordova, the Spanish city on the Guadalquivir that gave Rome the Seneca family.

Farrar shows how Spain shaped Roman letters, giving Rome emperors like Trajan and Hadrian and teachers like Quintilian. Seneca's father held knight's rank, and the son rose high at court. Farrar reads such lives with sympathy, honoring honest seeking after God in a world without the Christian faith he himself taught.
sentimental-tommy-the-story-of-his-boyho:
J. M. Barrie published this story of a boy's early years in 1896, after The Little Minister and A Window in Thrums had made his name. Tommy first appears at age five on a dirty London stair, in scant clothes that shame him. He will not beg, though hunger often tempts him.

His mother has warned him never to ask for food, and Tommy obeys with needless pride. Passing doors rich with the smell of fried fish, he calls out that he wants none of it. Barrie draws a proud, fanciful child whose lies and longings both spring from want, in prose both tender and sly.
sheila-of-big-wreck-cove-a-story-of-cape:
James A. Cooper wrote this Cape Cod tale, copyright as a book in 1922 after a serial run in 1921. A front picture by R. Emmett Owen shows a craft pointed out to Prudence. Contents open with Cap'n Ira and Prue, then the captain of the Seamew and a girl styled the Queen of Sheba.

Chapters follow a search for Ida May, a girl's own story, and a plot, before the scene settles at Big Wreck Cove. A new hand takes the helm there. Cooper mixes sea folk, young love, and hidden pasts in the salty, warm manner of his other Cape tales.
slavery-ordained-of-god:
Rev. Fred. A. Ross argues in Slavery Ordained of God that bondage forms part of the rule God set for fallen men in set states of life. The book is built from speeches he gave and letters he printed, not from stray pieces. Its text verse is Romans xiii. 1, on the powers that be. Ross speaks to men North and South who honor God's word.

His preface states one great idea, first put in a speech to the Presbyterian General Assembly at Buffalo on May 27, 1853. The North must learn, he says, that the master and slave tie is not sin in itself. The South must grant that bondage is an evil in some states of life, and that free and equal life ranks higher when its time comes.
spiritual-life-and-the-word-of-god: Emanuel Swedenborg, who lived from 1688 to 1772, wrote Spiritual Life and the Word of God, drawn from the Apocalypse Explained. The contents sort the work in four parts. The first treats how spiritual life is gained, the goods of charity, the shunning of evils, and the cleansing of the inside. The second walks through the commandments one by one, and the third treats the spoiling of good and truth in its kinds; the fourth treats the Divine Word and its senses.
stories-of-childhood:
Stories of Childhood forms one of the Little Classics volumes edited by Rossiter Johnson, printed by Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1914, with an 1875 copyright behind it. The set gathers short pieces about children by well-known hands.

The contents open with Ouida's A Dog of Flanders, where the boy Nello and the great dog Patrasche are left alone in the world, friends closer than brothers. John Ruskin's King of the Golden River follows. Then come pieces by Elizabeth Stuart Phelps and John Brown. Henry Kingsley and Rebecca Harding Davis add tales. Charles Dickens closes with A Child's Dream of a Star.
the-blossoming-rod:
Mary Stewart Cutting wrote a family story published in New York by A. L. Burt and Doubleday, Page. Mr Langshaw senses unusual preparations for his Christmas gift, as children ask him for change to pay for services. Money limits, the narrator says, run through the family's dearest hopes.

On the Friday before Christmas, Langshaw stops at a sporting-goods shop and finds a ten-dollar bill in his pocket, a debt repaid that day. A trout-rod in the window, cut from fifteen dollars to ten, tempts him at last. He worries over his son George, aged ten, who shirks duty to his mother. Longing, thrift, and fatherhood meet at Christmas.
the-elephant-god:
Gordon Gasserly's The Elephant God, printed at New York in 1921, is set in the Terai forest of India. Its contents open with a secret mission and a rogue elephant, then a girl of the Terai and the madness of Badshah. Later chapters name a rajah's palace, a Bhutia raid, the rescue of Noreen, and the making of a god.

Gasserly sets the book, with wry thanks, to a rogue elephant that slew men and women and taught him much. Love, fever rites for Kali, and jungle peril drive this Raj tale of soldiers and planters.
the-existence-of-god:
The Existence of God opens with a frank bar: proofs from metaphysics lie past most men's reach. Its author, unnamed in these pages, says he cannot open his eyes without seeing the art that shines through all nature; the least glance shows him the hand that made all. Thinkers may trace first principles, he owns, and that road is sure, but its very simplicity hides it from most.

Few can work in pure thought; most lean on sense and image. So the book turns to the path of nature's works. Plain words and short sections carry a case once famed across Europe.
the-flood:
Emile Zola wrote The Flood as a short tale told by an old farmer of Saint-Jory, a village on the Garonne near Toulouse. Louis Roubien, aged seventy, tells how his house was blessed.

Roubien counts his kin at table: his brother Pierre, his sister Agathe, his son Jacques and wife Rosie, three granddaughters, and babes down to ten months. He was the richest farmer in the parish, with no bad crop in memory. Pride in that full house sets the height from which the river's rise will cast them. Zola builds dread from plain, warm facts.
the-good-news-of-god: Charles Kingsley wrote The Good News of God. It is a book of sermons. Macmillan and Co. printed it in London in 1887. It was first transferred from Longman and Co. in 1863. It was reprinted many times since. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of sermons. The heads name The Beatific Vision and The Glory of the Cross. They name The Life of God, Worship, and De Profundis. They name The Race of Life and True Repentance. No sermon text is present.
the-lances-of-lynwood:
Charlotte M. Yonge's preface to this tale of chivalry hopes for one effect. The sketch should tempt young readers to Froissart's chronicle. His tomes' size should not deter them. The Orthon tale is copied nearly word for word from Froissart. It resembles German and Irish legends of household spirits. The old French life of Bertrand du Guesclin supplied more material. Enrique of Trastamare arrives disguised as a palmer in it. She apologizes for aging Henry of Lancaster. She made him a year or two older than his birth warrants.

Chapter I opens in Edward III's reign. England's interior presented a peaceful, prosperous aspect then. Turbulent spirits were occupied in foreign wars. Wise government established plenty and security at home. A second record of this tale in this set prints the same matter. Its preface and opening chapter are identical in what is shown.
the-leatherwood-god:
William Dean Howells bases his novel on a real Ohio religious imposture drawn from Judge Taneyhill narrative in an Ohio Valley series. A publisher note says the main events and drama follow that account, while details and inner lives are invented. Some speeches of the imposter Dylks come from a witness report.

Illustration captions show Dylks towering over followers in a temple at Leatherwood, hair tossed like a mane. Howells studies how a poor settlement could accept a man claim of godhood. Faith, pride, and hardship make neighbors defend a fraud they helped create.
the-life-and-romances-of-mrs-eliza-haywo: George Frisbie Whicher wrote his Columbia University monograph on Eliza Haywood life and romances in 1915. Only the title page and contents are present here. Chapters cover her life and her short romances of passion. The Duncan Campbell pamphlets, secret histories, scandal novels, and her place as a heroine of The Dunciad follow in the list. A bibliography, a chronological list, and an index close the plan. The study itself cannot be seen in this record.
the-little-house-in-the-fairy-wood:
Ethel Cook Eliot wrote The Little House in the Fairy Wood, a children's fantasy in nineteen chapters. Their titles include Magic in a Mist, At the Heart of a Tree, and The Beautiful Wicked Witch. Chapter one introduces Eric, a boy woken roughly at six in the morning by Mrs. Freg, who shakes him and the two boys sharing his bed and orders them all up. That ordinary morning, the narrator promises, will begin everything new for Eric.

The contents point toward a bright house in a wood, a Tree Mother, a wind hunt, birthdays, and spring wandering. Young readers get a gentle magic story that starts in a hard, crowded household and opens into an enchanted forest world.
the-merry-adventures-of-robin-hood:
Howard Pyle addresses the reader directly in the preface to The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood. He warns serious plodders who feel shame at mirth to close the book at once. His pages, he says, show sober folk of real history frisking in gay colors and motley. A stout, quick-tempered fellow goes by the name of Henry II, and a fair lady is bowed to as Queen Eleanor.

Pyle also promises the Sheriff of Nottingham, the Bishop of Hereford in rich clerical robes, and Richard of the Lion's Heart feasting beside Robin. His setting is not Fairyland but the land of Fancy, built from old ballads snipped, clipped, and tied together again. In that country flowers bloom forever and ale flows like a brook. Readers, young ones especially, are invited through the curtain into No-man's-land, where Robin's company lives the merriest of merry lives.
the-mystery-of-edwin-drood:
Charles Dickens's The Mystery of Edwin Drood lists twenty-three chapters in its contents, from The Dawn to A Gritty State of Things Comes On and The Dawn Again. Chapter I, The Dawn, opens in a drugged confusion. A man stares at an ancient English cathedral tower. He cannot understand how it stands before him. No spike of rusty iron rises in the real prospect between his eye and the tower.

The spike belongs to a vision. Cymbals clash, and a Sultan passes in long procession to his palace. Ten thousand scimitars flash, and dancing girls strew the way. The imagined spike waits there for Turkish robbers to be impaled. Rochester Castle illustrates the chapter in this printing, grounding the vision in Dickens's cathedral town of Cloisterham.
the-poetical-works-of-thomas-hood:
The Poetical Works of Thomas Hood, in an enlarged and revised edition from A. L. Burt Company of New York, opens with a biographical introduction by William Michael Rossetti. There were scarcely any events in Hood's life, Rossetti begins. Two conditions ruled it: life-long ill health, and a commercial failure that drove him abroad for a time. Beyond those, the outward facts of an upright, beneficial career offer little for the record.

Hood's father kept a publishing and bookselling business in London's Poultry, as a partner in Vernor, Hood, and Sharpe. A Scotchman who came up early, he reprinted old works and published Bloomfield's poems, dealing handsomely with him. He also wrote two novels himself. Rossetti wishes more were known of those forgotten tales. The son's questions about the piteous woman of his Bridge of Sighs still interest readers.
the-subterranean-brotherhood:
Julian Hawthorne's prison book opens with a poem called Footfalls, written in Atlanta Penitentiary in May 1913. The poet listens at night to a step overhead. It paces the cell, four paces from barred door to iron wall and back. He answers the unknown brother above him. The hunger for lost life goads that pacing. He knows that hunger too.

A contents list then maps the memoir's route. An introductory chapter leads off. The devil's antechamber and the road to oblivion follow. Initiation and routine come next. Some prison friends of the author's close the heads. Poem and contents together announce a first-hand account of federal prison life, written from inside the subterranean brotherhood of the barred and caged, pent from earth, sky, and stars.
the-thin-red-line-and-blue-blood: Arthur Griffiths, author of The Chronicles of Newgate, published The Thin Red Line in two volumes with Chapman and Hall in 1886; this record covers volume one. Only its title page and opening contents are present. Nine chapters begin with a commissary called, an arrest and interrogation, a mousetrap, a spider's web, and war fever, then move onto dangerous ground with an old acquaintance and a southern pearl. The headings sketch a military crime story of the Crimean era, but Griffiths's chapters themselves stay outside this record.
the-truce-of-god:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's Truce of God, published by George H. Doran in 1920 with decorations by Harold Sichel, opens on a grey, dreary Christmas Day that fell on a Saturday. The town at the hill's foot rejoices over a prosperous year, a fat steer dressed in the square amid heaps of fruit and vegetables. In his cliff-top castle the young overlord sulks and bites his nails. From Thursday evening to Monday morning the Church's Truce of God forbids his fighting.

For three full days each week his men-at-arms polish weapons and grow fat. Meanwhile his grudge against his cousin Philip, called the Black Beard, feeds on itself. The Bishop of Tours has come about scandalous reports: a lady has taken refuge with Philip. Rinehart, famous for mysteries, here writes a medieval tale of feud, sanctuary, and enforced peace.
unity-of-good: Mary Baker Eddy, author of Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, wrote Unity of Good. It was first copyrighted in 1887. The pages here give the title page and contents only, so the essays themselves do not appear. The contents list short pieces, several framed as questions. Caution in the Truth asks whether God can behold sin, sickness, and death. Seedtime and Harvest asks whether anything the senses grasp is real. Other titles include The Deep Things of God, A Colloquy, The Ego, and Soul.
young-robin-hood:
G. Manville Fenn wrote this children's tale of young Robin Hood. It opens on a forest road with a small boy riding behind a sour serving man named David. The boy wriggles on the slippery horse and teases David about his size. David threatens to pitch him into the brambles. The boy laughs that his father would punish such an act.

David then tries fear instead, asking if the dark forest scares him. The boy denies any fear at all. That bold start fits a future outlaw hero. Readers get a lively, talk-filled opening. Fenn keeps the scene light while danger waits in the trees.
